La Grenouille was a place of comfort, where she had no greater worries than ensuring that her mise en place was in order.
A sous-chef called back automatically to the expediter from the sauté station, "One salmon, one cog, heard!" The words sounded in rhythm to her rocking knife blade, chiffonading basil in a blur of motion on her cutting board. The smooth wood of the handle pivoted between thumb and forefinger in the expert motion known only to a seasoned cook.
Zoey's smooth motion grew faster. A bead of sweat formed on her forehead. The world seemed to fade into a blur of blacks and grays, no longer La Grenouille, but now somewhere else, dripping and stained with red. The ceramic tile wavered, and her knife flitted even faster.
Only one thing remained in Zoey's mind:
Meat. Meat, being hacked. Meat, torn and ripped in a fanged maw. Raw, dripping, bloody. Meat.
Her knife slipped through effortlessly, as it had been designed to, and dark crimson pooled around the vibrant green of the herbs and the busboy's hands were inches from her when her head slammed into the tile floor and darkness descended.

THE HOSPITAL VISIT WAS A RELATIVELY short one. After Zoey completed some paperwork, a middle-aged nurse brought her to an examination room and gave her a morphine shot for the pain. The nurse smelled of antiseptic and baby powder as she leaned over to tend the wound. She looked at her with careworn eyes and delicately ran the needle through Zoey's iodine-stained hand. "That's a dear. We'll have you stitched up in no time."
The seventeen stitches took less than an hour. Zoey's manager, Maurice, waited the whole time and was still waiting as Zoey emerged.
Maurice drove Zoey back to her apartment, the sec-and story of one of Southside's many townhouses. Large and leering, Maurice prattled the whole way, "My dear, you must be careful. I know how sharp you keep those knives. Very good for the kitchen, but so quick to cut if a hand slips but a little. You take some time to recover. We will see you in a few days, after those stitches come out." Feeling light-headed, Zoey simply watched as the scenery passed by on the trip from St. Mary's to her apartment. There was nothing to say. She nodded a goodbye as he pulled away. Leaning heavily on the ban-ister, Zoey ascended the flight of stairs up to her door.
Fumbling with her keys, she could hear her cat meowing on the inside. The door swung open, and Zoey stumbled through; little Misha, her calico, nudged her food dish across the kitchen tiles.
"Okay, Misha." Zoey gingerly opened the icebox and pulled out a small portion of roast, a leftover shed brought home from the restaurant earlier. She reached instinctively for her chef's knives. Gone. Maurice must have left them at her station. A chill swept over her. "It's okay. I'll get them tomorrow. I'll be okay." She would simply have to improvise. She plucked a fork from a nearby drawer with her off hand, picked apart the chunk of roast, and tipped the meat into Misha's bowl. The calico trotted over faithfully and set about to eating, purring all the while. Zoey knelt to scratch Misha as she ate. Her simple collar, decorated only with a St. Christopher's medal, tinkled against the food bowl. Zoey breathed deeply, muttering a simple prayer under her breath.
Misha wasn't her first cat, but the psychiatrist had said that maybe a new cat would help with the flash-backs. After what had happened to Sasha- -It was those tiny people, I know it. I can't prove it, but I know it. she hadn't been sure. Then, at the shelter, Misha had cried and cried when Zoey tried to walk away, and if nothing else, Zoey could never turn down an animal in need.
With Misha fed, Zoey studied the roast. Was she hungry? Meat. Red and glistening. She put it away, staggered to her bed. Her hand reached out for a knife but couldn't find one. Maybe it was for the best. She collapsed again, her vision darkening.

THE SEQUENCE WAS ALWAYS THE SAME.
The alley and the dumpster, the smell coming from the back. The rhythm of a thick cleaver through a thigh-bone, like Zoey had cut hundreds of times for marrow appetizers.
A little sel gris, a little roasted garlic, a few toast points...
But the smell? Like pork, but off. She had heard the rumors of the strange dishes served by diminutive waiters who called themselves "Tcho-Tchos," just a few doors down, but she simply attributed the tales to the cutthroat nature of the culinary world. A restaurant lived and died by its reputation, after all.
She still didn't know why she had cut through the alley that night. To get home faster? A change of pace?
The door had hung open, and two small men with toothy grins had stared back out at her. "Long pig" shed heard it called, but it was no pig on their butcher's table.

It was a young man: a blond-haired twenty-something, dead and drained of blood, his thigh bone split and ready for the broiler.
A flash of red and silver. The toothy murderers slashed open across the restaurant floor. Her favorite knife dripping as she gasped in horror and incredulity.
Then, running through the blackness of the Arkham streets. Collapsing in the shower, reciting "Rejoice Mary" over and over again, as the water ran red down the drain.

THE DREAMS HAD NOT STARTED THAT first night, despite the trauma, despite the blood and the realization of what she'd done. She'd had no dreams, no fainting spells. She'd been dead inside, numb to the terror she'd seen.
And it had been terrible. It hadn't been the first time the Lord had directed her knife, but somehow it had been the worst. And the Lord was silent now.
It was in one of Father Alexandros's liturgies that the dreams had first come. Maybe the sanctuary was too warm that day. Maybe it was the flashing of the knife as he cut the lamb from the host. Maybe it was all just too much to comprehend.
Alexandros lifted the bread to his lips and kissed it. "He gave it to them, and •
said "Take, eat: this is my body...»
Zoey's resolute hands gripped the rail of the pew in front of her.
Her knuckles whitened. Her face followed suit.
Alexandros continued, raising a chalice filled with dark crimson, "Drink ye all of it; for this is my blood.."
Parishioners began filing into line to partake. It was all Zoey could do to stumble out into the vestibule, gasping for air. That was the first night. The first night that the dreams came.

ZOEY SAT UP. HER VISION HAD CLEARED.
Misha hopped into her lap, but Zoey lifted her and placed her on the bed, standing. "I have work to do," she said.
She pulled on her shoes and coat, careful of her stitches. It was dark outside. That was best. She didn't want anyone to see while she did her work. No knives.
The Lord didn't want her to use her knives tonight, then?
He'd sent the vision, the one that had made her cut her-self. It was His plan that had sent her to the hospital.
She would start her hunt in that direction. In time, she would find the evil that the Lord had commanded her to destroy. She didn't have her knives, but that was all right. She would simply have to improvise.

Slide 1: Introduction to Acid Rain
- Definition of acid rain: Precipitation with a pH level lower than 5.6, caused by the atmospheric deposition of sulfuric and nitric acids
- Formation process: Emissions of sulfur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) from human activities (e.g., burning fossil fuels) react with water, oxygen, and other chemicals in the atmosphere to form acidic compounds
- Consequences: Acid rain has negative effects on waterways, forests, wildlife, architecture, and human health

Slide 2: Causes of Acid Rain in the Great Lakes Region
- Industrial and power plant emissions: Coal-fired power plants and manufacturing facilities are major sources of SO2 and NOx emissions in the region
- Transportation: Vehicle exhaust contributes to NOx emissions
- Geography and weather patterns: The region’s prevailing winds and lake-effect weather patterns can transport and deposit air pollutants within and across state and international borders
- Lake-air interactions: The Great Lakes influence regional weather by modifying air temperature, humidity, and wind patterns, potentially exacerbating acid rain issues

Slide 3: Impact of Acid Rain on the Great Lakes Ecosystem
- Altered pH levels: Acid rain lowers the pH of water bodies, making them more acidic and potentially toxic to aquatic life
- Forest stress: Acid rain can leach nutrients like calcium and magnesium from the soil, weaken trees, and make them more susceptible to pests, disease, and climate stressors
- Wildlife impacts: Changes in vegetation, water chemistry, and food availability can disrupt ecosystems and harm species dependent on the affected habitat

Slide 4: Impact on Human Health and Recreation
- Toxic metals: Acid rain can promote the release of naturally occurring toxic metals (e.g., mercury, lead) from the soil, contaminating water sources and fish
- Drinking water: Acidic water sources can corrode pipes and release harmful metals like lead, posing risks to human health
- Recreation across the Great Lakes: Swimming, boating, and fishing activities can be affected by water quality, with fish consumption advisories due to contamination

Slide 5: Acid Rain Regulations and Policy
- The Clean Air Act (CAA): U.S. legislation aimed at reducing emissions of air pollutants, including SO2 and NOx
- Amendments to the CAA: The 1990 amendments established the Acid Rain Program, a cap-and-trade system designed to reduce national SO2 and NOx emissions
- International cooperation: The Canada-United States Air Quality Agreement (1991) aims to address transboundary air pollution, including acid rain-causing emissions


Slide 6: Solutions and Future Challenges
- Clean energy transition: Shifting toward renewable energy sources (e.g., solar, wind, nuclear) can help reduce emissions contributing to acid rain
- Technology advancements: Improved methods for reducing emissions from existing sources, such as carbon capture and storage or scrubber technology
- Ecosystem recovery: Reforestation and ecosystem restoration efforts can help recovery from acid rain damage, though long-term monitoring is necessary

Slide 7: Conclusion
- The importance of maintaining and strengthening regulations to address SO2 and NOx emissions for the protection of human health, ecosystems, and recreational activities in the Great Lakes region
- The potential exacerbation of acid rain issues due to climate change, requiring continued attention and enhanced, cooperative efforts
- Ongoing collaboration between industry, government, communities, and international partners is crucial for effective acid rain mitigation and ecosystem recovery

Background
This portion of the lab section involved creating a genomic library using a streptomycin
resistant strain of E.coli top10 (4537 bp) as the genomic DNA which will be incorporated into
puc19 plasmid (2686 bp) vector as proposed earlier in PART B proposal document.
To achieve the proposed plan, E.coli strain top10 (4537 bp) will serve as the genomic strain that
will be the source of streptomycin resistance rspL gene. The FastDigest HindIII (thermo
scientific) digested fragment will be insert into a digested pUC19 plasmid vector (2686 bp)
utilizing ligation process. Once ligated, the product will be transformed with Mach1 chemically
competent cells (O.D. value = 0.77). To confirm the success of ligation the transformed product
will be plated on Ampillicin/X-gal/IPTG plates and the white colonies will then be streaked onto
streptomycin plates to verify the rspl gene streptomycin resistance property.
As per the proposal, digesting the bacterial strains with similar digestion enzyme (HindIII) prior
to ligation followed by transformation would have ideally given the genomic library however,
throughout the project certain decisions were changed based on the results which will be
thoroughly covered in this document along with the solutions taken to troubleshoot the
mistakes.
Methods/Materials
Isolation of genomic DNA and plasmid DNA:
To start with the procedure of creating a genomic library from E.coli strain Top10 and plasmid
pUC19, 5 mL genomic DNA (Top10) and 3 mL plasmid pUC19 was isolated using GeneJET
genomic DNA purification kit (lot 01319594) and GeneJET plasmid Mini prep kit (lot 01218820)
respectively.

Genomic material A260/A280 A260/A230 DNA Conc. (ng/µL)

Discussion
The primary objective of this project was to create a genomic library using a streptomycinresistant strain of E.coli Top10 (4537 bp) as the genomic DNA, incorporating it into a pUC19
plasmid (2686 bp) vector (Cirino et al., 2003). The successful construction of this genomic
library was expected to confer streptomycin resistance to a recipient E.coli strain Mach1
through the functional selection of the rspL gene (Hanahan, 1983). However, throughout the
experiment, several challenges were encountered, leading to changes in the experimental
design and troubleshooting of errors.
An initial gel electrophoresis performed to confirm the presence of the rspL gene after digestion
of genomic DNA with BamHI resulted in no visible bands. This was primarily due to the low
concentration of the originally isolated genomic Top10 DNA (33.2 ng/µL), which was further
diluted during the digestion reaction and loading of the gel (Inoue et al., 1990). This
concentration was below the minimum detection limit required for the INtRON RedSafeTM
nucleic acid stain to work efficiently (50 ng/µL). As a consequence, no bands were detected,
and the experiment had to be repeated with a new and cleaned up genomic DNA sample.
Subsequent gel electrophoresis performed after digesting the cleaned-up genomic DNA with
BamHI showed successful digestion of the genomic Top10 DNA, as evidenced by a shorter
smear in comparison to the uncut band of the genomic DNA (Sorek et al., 2013). In addition, the
plasmid pUC19 showed two very faint bands after digestion with BamHI, indicating appropriate
digestion of the plasmid as well.
Part B write up 15
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
A ligation reaction was set up using a 1:1 ratio for cut genomic Top10 DNA (insert) and cut
plasmid pUC19 (vector) (Chen & Dubnau, 2004). After overnight incubation at 4 °C, the ligated
product was transformed into Mach1 chemically competent cells. The initial transformation
results were inconclusive due to contamination observed in the positive control plate.
Moreover, the second transformation attempt resulted in an unsuccessful transformation due
to inefficient uptake of DNA by the host organism, which might have been caused by several
factors, such as improper preparation of competent cells, issues concerning the ligation
reaction, or the transformation protocol itself (Inoue et al., 1990).
To increase the likelihood of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene, a third gel
electrophoresis was performed using HindIII in addition to BamHI for digesting both genomic
Top10 DNA and plasmid pUC19 (Cirino et al., 2003). The use of two different enzymes would
increase the accuracy of the construct and facilitate the incorporation of the desired fragment
into the plasmid (Hanahan, 1983).
Based on the information provided by the restriction analyzer, the BamHI enzyme cuts at two
different sites on genomic DNA (180 and 2865), producing large fragments that appeared as a
smear in the gel electrophoresis images (Sorek et al., 2013). HindIII was introduced to cut at an
additional site (4130) on genomic DNA, increasing the likelihood that the fragment containing
the rspL gene would be successfully incorporated into the plasmid (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
In summary, the construction of a genomic library using E.coli Top10 genomic DNA and pUC19
plasmid DNA encountered several challenges throughout the experiment, including low DNA
concentrations, contamination, and inefficient transformation (Inoue et al., 1990). The
introduction of the HindIII enzyme in addition to BamHI for restriction digestion was expected
to increase the probability of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene (Cirino et al., 2003).
Furthermore, troubleshooting in each area of competent cells preparation, ligation reaction,
and transformation protocol can assist in identifying and rectifying these challenges, such as reevaluating the insert-to-vector ratio, incubation time, and temperature for the ligation reaction
or testing and optimizing various transformation conditions (Hanahan, 1983).
For this experiment, the most likely problem would be with transformation. It could be
optimized and modified by making changes mentioned below:
a. Temperature and duration: Confirm that the heat shock conditions (e.g. 42°C for 30-45
seconds) are appropriate for your cells (Inoue et al., 1990).
b. Recovery duration: Allow adequate time (usually 1 hour) for the cells to recover and express
the antibiotic resistance marker (Sorek et al., 2013).
c. Optimal antibiotic concentration: Ensure the appropriate concentration of streptomycin for
selection is used on the plates. Too high or low of a concentration may result in inadequate
selection (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
Part B write up 16
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
In addition to the technical challenges faced during the genomic library construction, human
errors could also have contributed to the unsuccessful or inconclusive results. These errors can
occur in sample handling, reagent preparation, equipment usage, and protocol execution. Such
errors may include:
1. Cross-contamination: During handling of samples, there is potential for cross-contamination
between different DNA samples or between the samples and reagents, leading to undesired
results (Inoue et al., 1990).
2. Reagent preparation: Errors can occur while preparing various reagents such as buffers,
enzyme solutions, or antibiotics. These could include inaccurate measurement or mixing of
components, resulting in incorrect concentrations that can affect experimental outcomes
(Sorek et al., 2013).
3. Pipetting errors: Inaccurate pipetting can lead to incorrect volumes being dispensed, resulting
in the incorrect sample or reagent concentration, which affects the outcome of experiments
(Hanahan, 1983).
4. Equipment usage: Improper operation, maintenance, or calibration of laboratory equipment
can generate unreliable or inconsistent results. For instance, inaccurate temperature settings
for incubation or heat shock can affect the transformation efficiency (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
To minimize human errors, it is essential to maintain good laboratory practices, maintaining
proper organization of the workspace, labeling samples accurately, and double-checking
reagent concentrations. Additionally, regularly calibrating and maintaining equipment,
following established protocols carefully, and incorporating appropriate controls into
experiments will help reduce the occurrence of human errors and enhance the overall success
of the genomic library construction process.
Future experiments can investigate alternative restriction enzymes, plasmid vectors, and
competent cell strains to improve the overall success of the genomic library construction
process (Cirino et al., 2003). Moreover, ensuring a suitable recovery time for transformed cells,
providing a nutrient-rich medium during recovery, using appropriate plating methods and
conditions, and including positive and negative controls in each transformation experiment will
aid in enhancing the efficiency of the genomic library construction and subsequent functional
selection of the streptomycin resistance-conferring rspL gene (Hanahan, 1983).
Conclusion
Part B write up 17
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
In conclusion, the construction of a genomic library using E.coli Top10 genomic DNA and pUC19
plasmid DNA proved to be challenging due to several factors, including low DNA
concentrations, contamination, and inefficient transformation. Optimization of the
transformation process, selection of alternative restriction enzymes, plasmid vectors, and
competent cell strains could enhance the overall success of the genomic library construction
and subsequent functional selection of the streptomycin resistance-conferring rspL gene.
Future experiments should also emphasize proper controls, recovery conditions, and nutrientrich media to improve the efficiency of this process.

Background
This portion of the lab section involved creating a genomic library using a streptomycin
resistant strain of E.coli top10 (4537 bp) as the genomic DNA which will be incorporated into
puc19 plasmid (2686 bp) vector as proposed earlier in PART B proposal document.
To achieve the proposed plan, E.coli strain top10 (4537 bp) will serve as the genomic strain that
will be the source of streptomycin resistance rspL gene. The FastDigest HindIII (thermo
scientific) digested fragment will be insert into a digested pUC19 plasmid vector (2686 bp)
utilizing ligation process. Once ligated, the product will be transformed with Mach1 chemically
competent cells (O.D. value = 0.77). To confirm the success of ligation the transformed product
will be plated on Ampillicin/X-gal/IPTG plates and the white colonies will then be streaked onto
streptomycin plates to verify the rspl gene streptomycin resistance property.
As per the proposal, digesting the bacterial strains with similar digestion enzyme (HindIII) prior
to ligation followed by transformation would have ideally given the genomic library however,
throughout the project certain decisions were changed based on the results which will be
thoroughly covered in this document along with the solutions taken to troubleshoot the
mistakes.
Methods/Materials
Isolation of genomic DNA and plasmid DNA:
To start with the procedure of creating a genomic library from E.coli strain Top10 and plasmid
pUC19, 5 mL genomic DNA (Top10) and 3 mL plasmid pUC19 was isolated using GeneJET
genomic DNA purification kit (lot 01319594) and GeneJET plasmid Mini prep kit (lot 01218820)
respectively.

Image 9: Information regarding the total length of the plasmid DNA using restriction analyzer
Part B write up 14
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
The above image provides information related to the pUC19 plasmid DNA that is 2686 bp long.
The tool used for this was restriction analyzer. It also shows that BamHI cuts at 662 position on
plasmid DNA and HindIII cuts at 632 positions. Since we are using two different enzymes, there
is a better chance that our fragment contains rspL gene.
Discussion
The primary objective of this project was to create a genomic library using a streptomycinresistant strain of E.coli Top10 (4537 bp) as the genomic DNA, incorporating it into a pUC19
plasmid (2686 bp) vector (Cirino et al., 2003). The successful construction of this genomic
library was expected to confer streptomycin resistance to a recipient E.coli strain Mach1
through the functional selection of the rspL gene (Hanahan, 1983). However, throughout the
experiment, several challenges were encountered, leading to changes in the experimental
design and troubleshooting of errors.
An initial gel electrophoresis performed to confirm the presence of the rspL gene after digestion
of genomic DNA with BamHI resulted in no visible bands. This was primarily due to the low
concentration of the originally isolated genomic Top10 DNA (33.2 ng/µL), which was further
diluted during the digestion reaction and loading of the gel (Inoue et al., 1990). This
concentration was below the minimum detection limit required for the INtRON RedSafeTM
nucleic acid stain to work efficiently (50 ng/µL). As a consequence, no bands were detected,
and the experiment had to be repeated with a new and cleaned up genomic DNA sample.
Subsequent gel electrophoresis performed after digesting the cleaned-up genomic DNA with
BamHI showed successful digestion of the genomic Top10 DNA, as evidenced by a shorter
smear in comparison to the uncut band of the genomic DNA (Sorek et al., 2013). In addition, the
plasmid pUC19 showed two very faint bands after digestion with BamHI, indicating appropriate
digestion of the plasmid as well.
Part B write up 15
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
A ligation reaction was set up using a 1:1 ratio for cut genomic Top10 DNA (insert) and cut
plasmid pUC19 (vector) (Chen & Dubnau, 2004). After overnight incubation at 4 °C, the ligated
product was transformed into Mach1 chemically competent cells. The initial transformation
results were inconclusive due to contamination observed in the positive control plate.
Moreover, the second transformation attempt resulted in an unsuccessful transformation due
to inefficient uptake of DNA by the host organism, which might have been caused by several
factors, such as improper preparation of competent cells, issues concerning the ligation
reaction, or the transformation protocol itself (Inoue et al., 1990).
To increase the likelihood of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene, a third gel
electrophoresis was performed using HindIII in addition to BamHI for digesting both genomic
Top10 DNA and plasmid pUC19 (Cirino et al., 2003). The use of two different enzymes would
increase the accuracy of the construct and facilitate the incorporation of the desired fragment
into the plasmid (Hanahan, 1983).
Based on the information provided by the restriction analyzer, the BamHI enzyme cuts at two
different sites on genomic DNA (180 and 2865), producing large fragments that appeared as a
smear in the gel electrophoresis images (Sorek et al., 2013). HindIII was introduced to cut at an
additional site (4130) on genomic DNA, increasing the likelihood that the fragment containing
the rspL gene would be successfully incorporated into the plasmid (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
In summary, the construction of a genomic library using E.coli Top10 genomic DNA and pUC19
plasmid DNA encountered several challenges throughout the experiment, including low DNA
concentrations, contamination, and inefficient transformation (Inoue et al., 1990). The
introduction of the HindIII enzyme in addition to BamHI for restriction digestion was expected
to increase the probability of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene (Cirino et al., 2003).
Furthermore, troubleshooting in each area of competent cells preparation, ligation reaction,
and transformation protocol can assist in identifying and rectifying these challenges, such as reevaluating the insert-to-vector ratio, incubation time, and temperature for the ligation reaction
or testing and optimizing various transformation conditions (Hanahan, 1983).
For this experiment, the most likely problem would be with transformation. It could be
optimized and modified by making changes mentioned below:
a. Temperature and duration: Confirm that the heat shock conditions (e.g. 42°C for 30-45
seconds) are appropriate for your cells (Inoue et al., 1990).
b. Recovery duration: Allow adequate time (usually 1 hour) for the cells to recover and express
the antibiotic resistance marker (Sorek et al., 2013).
c. Optimal antibiotic concentration: Ensure the appropriate concentration of streptomycin for
selection is used on the plates. Too high or low of a concentration may result in inadequate
selection (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
Part B write up 16
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
In addition to the technical challenges faced during the genomic library construction, human
errors could also have contributed to the unsuccessful or inconclusive results. These errors can
occur in sample handling, reagent preparation, equipment usage, and protocol execution. Such
errors may include:
1. Cross-contamination: During handling of samples, there is potential for cross-contamination
between different DNA samples or between the samples and reagents, leading to undesired
results (Inoue et al., 1990).
2. Reagent preparation: Errors can occur while preparing various reagents such as buffers,
enzyme solutions, or antibiotics. These could include inaccurate measurement or mixing of
components, resulting in incorrect concentrations that can affect experimental outcomes
(Sorek et al., 2013).
3. Pipetting errors: Inaccurate pipetting can lead to incorrect volumes being dispensed, resulting
in the incorrect sample or reagent concentration, which affects the outcome of experiments
(Hanahan, 1983).
4. Equipment usage: Improper operation, maintenance, or calibration of laboratory equipment
can generate unreliable or inconsistent results. For instance, inaccurate temperature settings
for incubation or heat shock can affect the transformation efficiency (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
To minimize human errors, it is essential to maintain good laboratory practices, maintaining
proper organization of the workspace, labeling samples accurately, and double-checking
reagent concentrations. Additionally, regularly calibrating and maintaining equipment,
following established protocols carefully, and incorporating appropriate controls into
experiments will help reduce the occurrence of human errors and enhance the overall success
of the genomic library construction process.
Future experiments can investigate alternative restriction enzymes, plasmid vectors, and
competent cell strains to improve the overall success of the genomic library construction
process (Cirino et al., 2003). Moreover, ensuring a suitable recovery time for transformed cells,
providing a nutrient-rich medium during recovery, using appropriate plating methods and
conditions, and including positive and negative controls in each transformation experiment will
aid in enhancing the efficiency of the genomic library construction and subsequent functional
selection of the streptomycin resistance-conferring rspL gene (Hanahan, 1983).
Conclusion
Part B write up 17
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
In conclusion, the construction of a genomic library using E.coli Top10 genomic DNA and pUC19
plasmid DNA proved to be challenging due to several factors, including low DNA
concentrations, contamination, and inefficient transformation. Optimization of the
transformation process, selection of alternative restriction enzymes, plasmid vectors, and
competent cell strains could enhance the overall success of the genomic library construction
and subsequent functional selection of the streptomycin resistance-conferring rspL gene.
Future experiments should also emphasize proper controls, recovery conditions, and nutrientrich media to improve the efficiency of this process.

Discussion
The primary objective of this project was to create a genomic library using a streptomycinresistant strain of E.coli Top10 (4537 bp) as the genomic DNA, incorporating it into a pUC19
plasmid (2686 bp) vector (Cirino et al., 2003). The successful construction of this genomic
library was expected to confer streptomycin resistance to a recipient E.coli strain Mach1
through the functional selection of the rspL gene (Hanahan, 1983). However, throughout the
experiment, several challenges were encountered, leading to changes in the experimental
design and troubleshooting of errors.
An initial gel electrophoresis performed to confirm the presence of the rspL gene after digestion
of genomic DNA with BamHI resulted in no visible bands. This was primarily due to the low
concentration of the originally isolated genomic Top10 DNA (33.2 ng/µL), which was further
diluted during the digestion reaction and loading of the gel (Inoue et al., 1990). This
concentration was below the minimum detection limit required for the INtRON RedSafeTM
nucleic acid stain to work efficiently (50 ng/µL). As a consequence, no bands were detected,
and the experiment had to be repeated with a new and cleaned up genomic DNA sample.
Subsequent gel electrophoresis performed after digesting the cleaned-up genomic DNA with
BamHI showed successful digestion of the genomic Top10 DNA, as evidenced by a shorter
smear in comparison to the uncut band of the genomic DNA (Sorek et al., 2013). In addition, the
plasmid pUC19 showed two very faint bands after digestion with BamHI, indicating appropriate
digestion of the plasmid as well.
Part B write up 15
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
A ligation reaction was set up using a 1:1 ratio for cut genomic Top10 DNA (insert) and cut
plasmid pUC19 (vector) (Chen & Dubnau, 2004). After overnight incubation at 4 °C, the ligated
product was transformed into Mach1 chemically competent cells. The initial transformation
results were inconclusive due to contamination observed in the positive control plate.
Moreover, the second transformation attempt resulted in an unsuccessful transformation due
to inefficient uptake of DNA by the host organism, which might have been caused by several
factors, such as improper preparation of competent cells, issues concerning the ligation
reaction, or the transformation protocol itself (Inoue et al., 1990).
To increase the likelihood of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene, a third gel
electrophoresis was performed using HindIII in addition to BamHI for digesting both genomic
Top10 DNA and plasmid pUC19 (Cirino et al., 2003). The use of two different enzymes would
increase the accuracy of the construct and facilitate the incorporation of the desired fragment
into the plasmid (Hanahan, 1983).
Based on the information provided by the restriction analyzer, the BamHI enzyme cuts at two
different sites on genomic DNA (180 and 2865), producing large fragments that appeared as a
smear in the gel electrophoresis images (Sorek et al., 2013). HindIII was introduced to cut at an
additional site (4130) on genomic DNA, increasing the likelihood that the fragment containing
the rspL gene would be successfully incorporated into the plasmid (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
In summary, the construction of a genomic library using E.coli Top10 genomic DNA and pUC19
plasmid DNA encountered several challenges throughout the experiment, including low DNA
concentrations, contamination, and inefficient transformation (Inoue et al., 1990). The
introduction of the HindIII enzyme in addition to BamHI for restriction digestion was expected
to increase the probability of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene (Cirino et al., 2003).
Furthermore, troubleshooting in each area of competent cells preparation, ligation reaction,
and transformation protocol can assist in identifying and rectifying these challenges, such as reevaluating the insert-to-vector ratio, incubation time, and temperature for the ligation reaction
or testing and optimizing various transformation conditions (Hanahan, 1983).
For this experiment, the most likely problem would be with transformation. It could be
optimized and modified by making changes mentioned below:
a. Temperature and duration: Confirm that the heat shock conditions (e.g. 42°C for 30-45
seconds) are appropriate for your cells (Inoue et al., 1990).
b. Recovery duration: Allow adequate time (usually 1 hour) for the cells to recover and express
the antibiotic resistance marker (Sorek et al., 2013).
c. Optimal antibiotic concentration: Ensure the appropriate concentration of streptomycin for
selection is used on the plates. Too high or low of a concentration may result in inadequate
selection (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
Part B write up 16
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
In addition to the technical challenges faced during the genomic library construction, human
errors could also have contributed to the unsuccessful or inconclusive results. These errors can
occur in sample handling, reagent preparation, equipment usage, and protocol execution. Such
errors may include:
1. Cross-contamination: During handling of samples, there is potential for cross-contamination
between different DNA samples or between the samples and reagents, leading to undesired
results (Inoue et al., 1990).
2. Reagent preparation: Errors can occur while preparing various reagents such as buffers,
enzyme solutions, or antibiotics. These could include inaccurate measurement or mixing of
components, resulting in incorrect concentrations that can affect experimental outcomes
(Sorek et al., 2013).
3. Pipetting errors: Inaccurate pipetting can lead to incorrect volumes being dispensed, resulting
in the incorrect sample or reagent concentration, which affects the outcome of experiments
(Hanahan, 1983).
4. Equipment usage: Improper operation, maintenance, or calibration of laboratory equipment
can generate unreliable or inconsistent results. For instance, inaccurate temperature settings
for incubation or heat shock can affect the transformation efficiency (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
To minimize human errors, it is essential to maintain good laboratory practices, maintaining
proper organization of the workspace, labeling samples accurately, and double-checking
reagent concentrations. Additionally, regularly calibrating and maintaining equipment,
following established protocols carefully, and incorporating appropriate controls into
experiments will help reduce the occurrence of human errors and enhance the overall success
of the genomic library construction process.
Future experiments can investigate alternative restriction enzymes, plasmid vectors, and
competent cell strains to improve the overall success of the genomic library construction
process (Cirino et al., 2003). Moreover, ensuring a suitable recovery time for transformed cells,
providing a nutrient-rich medium during recovery, using appropriate plating methods and
conditions, and including positive and negative controls in each transformation experiment will
aid in enhancing the efficiency of the genomic library construction and subsequent functional
selection of the streptomycin resistance-conferring rspL gene (Hanahan, 1983).
Conclusion
Part B write up 17
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
In conclusion, the construction of a genomic library using E.coli Top10 genomic DNA and pUC19
plasmid DNA proved to be challenging due to several factors, including low DNA
concentrations, contamination, and inefficient transformation. Optimization of the
transformation process, selection of alternative restriction enzymes, plasmid vectors, and
competent cell strains could enhance the overall success of the genomic library construction
and subsequent functional selection of the streptomycin resistance-conferring rspL gene.
Future experiments should also emphasize proper controls, recovery conditions, and nutrientrich media to improve the efficiency of this process.

The Principles of the Metabolist Movement and Contemporary Urbanism

From the Industrial Revolution to the present day, humanity has faced growing challenges related to urbanization, densification, and sustainability. The principles and ideals of the Metabolist movement have much to offer the contemporary built environment, particularly as societies grapple with these challenges. By drawing on the example of the 1970 Osaka Expo and the innovative solutions it offered to urban challenges, this essay argues that architects and urban planners must keep the Metabolist emphasis on flexible, adaptable, and socially-integrated design at the forefront of their efforts. Specifically, by prioritizing the repurposing, refurbishing, and careful consideration of existing built environments, designers can create a more sustainable and adaptive urban landscape that draws on the successes of the past while innovating for the future.

The Metabolist movement emerged in post-war Japan in response to the growing challenges of urban densification and the need for flexible, adaptable architecture. The movement emphasized the need for buildings and infrastructure to be designed in a way that could easily be expanded or modified as the needs of the inhabitants changed over time. The movement was deeply influential in the design of the 1970 Osaka Expo, which sought to showcase innovative and sustainable solutions to urban challenges.

At the heart of the Metabolist movement was a deep commitment to flexible, adaptable design. This principle is particularly relevant in the contemporary urban context. With cities around the world facing growing challenges related to densification and sustainability, designers must embrace the flexible and adaptable approach advocated by Metabolism in order to create a built environment that is responsive to changing needs and circumstances.

One key way that the principles of the Metabolist movement can be applied in the contemporary urban context is through the repurposing and refurbishing of existing built environments. By prioritizing the careful consideration of existing structures and infrastructure, designers can create sustainable and adaptive urban environments that draw on the legacies of the past. This approach can help to reduce the environmental impact of urban growth and support the long-term viability of the built environment.

The example of the 1970 Osaka Expo provides a powerful demonstration of the potential of the Metabolist approach in action. The Expo aimed to address a range of social and environmental challenges, including issues of urbanization, housing, and sustainability. By
emphasizing the use of innovative materials and technologies, the Expo showcased the potential for the built environment to serve as a platform for social and environmental progress.

Importantly, the success of the Expo was due in large part to the flexible and adaptable design principles advocated by the Metabolist movement. The Expo structures were designed to be easily disassembled and reused after the event, demonstrating the potential for sustainable and adaptable infrastructure to support long-term urban growth.

As cities around the world continue to face the challenges of densification and sustainability, the principles of the Metabolist movement offer a compelling framework for urban design and planning. By prioritizing social and environmental values and embracing flexible and adaptable approaches to urban design, architects and urban planners can create vibrant and sustainable built environments that support the needs of contemporary society while drawing on the legacies of the past.

In conclusion, the Metabolist movement provides a powerful example of how the principles of flexible and adaptable urban design can be used to address the challenges of urbanization and sustainability. By drawing on the example of the 1970 Osaka Expo and emphasizing the importance of repurposing and refurbishing existing built environments, architects and urban planners can create sustainable and adaptive urban landscapes that support the long-term viability of the built environment.

Discussion
The primary objective of this project was to create a genomic library using a streptomycinresistant strain of E.coli Top10 (4537 bp) as the genomic DNA, incorporating it into a pUC19
plasmid (2686 bp) vector (Cirino et al., 2003). The successful construction of this genomic
library was expected to confer streptomycin resistance to a recipient E.coli strain Mach1
through the functional selection of the rspL gene (Hanahan, 1983). However, throughout the
experiment, several challenges were encountered, leading to changes in the experimental
design and troubleshooting of errors.
An initial gel electrophoresis performed to confirm the presence of the rspL gene after digestion
of genomic DNA with BamHI resulted in no visible bands. This was primarily due to the low
concentration of the originally isolated genomic Top10 DNA (33.2 ng/µL), which was further
diluted during the digestion reaction and loading of the gel (Inoue et al., 1990). This
concentration was below the minimum detection limit required for the INtRON RedSafeTM
nucleic acid stain to work efficiently (50 ng/µL). As a consequence, no bands were detected,
and the experiment had to be repeated with a new and cleaned up genomic DNA sample.
Subsequent gel electrophoresis performed after digesting the cleaned-up genomic DNA with
BamHI showed successful digestion of the genomic Top10 DNA, as evidenced by a shorter
smear in comparison to the uncut band of the genomic DNA (Sorek et al., 2013). In addition, the
plasmid pUC19 showed two very faint bands after digestion with BamHI, indicating appropriate
digestion of the plasmid as well.
Part B write up 15
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
A ligation reaction was set up using a 1:1 ratio for cut genomic Top10 DNA (insert) and cut
plasmid pUC19 (vector) (Chen & Dubnau, 2004). After overnight incubation at 4 °C, the ligated
product was transformed into Mach1 chemically competent cells. The initial transformation
results were inconclusive due to contamination observed in the positive control plate.
Moreover, the second transformation attempt resulted in an unsuccessful transformation due
to inefficient uptake of DNA by the host organism, which might have been caused by several
factors, such as improper preparation of competent cells, issues concerning the ligation
reaction, or the transformation protocol itself (Inoue et al., 1990).
To increase the likelihood of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene, a third gel
electrophoresis was performed using HindIII in addition to BamHI for digesting both genomic
Top10 DNA and plasmid pUC19 (Cirino et al., 2003). The use of two different enzymes would
increase the accuracy of the construct and facilitate the incorporation of the desired fragment
into the plasmid (Hanahan, 1983).
Based on the information provided by the restriction analyzer, the BamHI enzyme cuts at two
different sites on genomic DNA (180 and 2865), producing large fragments that appeared as a
smear in the gel electrophoresis images (Sorek et al., 2013). HindIII was introduced to cut at an
additional site (4130) on genomic DNA, increasing the likelihood that the fragment containing
the rspL gene would be successfully incorporated into the plasmid (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
In summary, the construction of a genomic library using E.coli Top10 genomic DNA and pUC19
plasmid DNA encountered several challenges throughout the experiment, including low DNA
concentrations, contamination, and inefficient transformation (Inoue et al., 1990). The
introduction of the HindIII enzyme in addition to BamHI for restriction digestion was expected
to increase the probability of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene (Cirino et al., 2003).
Furthermore, troubleshooting in each area of competent cells preparation, ligation reaction,
and transformation protocol can assist in identifying and rectifying these challenges, such as reevaluating the insert-to-vector ratio, incubation time, and temperature for the ligation reaction
or testing and optimizing various transformation conditions (Hanahan, 1983).
For this experiment, the most likely problem would be with transformation. It could be
optimized and modified by making changes mentioned below:
a. Temperature and duration: Confirm that the heat shock conditions (e.g. 42°C for 30-45
seconds) are appropriate for your cells (Inoue et al., 1990).
b. Recovery duration: Allow adequate time (usually 1 hour) for the cells to recover and express
the antibiotic resistance marker (Sorek et al., 2013).
c. Optimal antibiotic concentration: Ensure the appropriate concentration of streptomycin for
selection is used on the plates. Too high or low of a concentration may result in inadequate
selection (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).

In addition to the technical challenges faced during the genomic library construction, human
errors could also have contributed to the unsuccessful or inconclusive results. These errors can
occur in sample handling, reagent preparation, equipment usage, and protocol execution. Such
errors may include:
1. Cross-contamination: During handling of samples, there is potential for cross-contamination
between different DNA samples or between the samples and reagents, leading to undesired
results (Inoue et al., 1990).
2. Reagent preparation: Errors can occur while preparing various reagents such as buffers,
enzyme solutions, or antibiotics. These could include inaccurate measurement or mixing of
components, resulting in incorrect concentrations that can affect experimental outcomes
(Sorek et al., 2013).
3. Pipetting errors: Inaccurate pipetting can lead to incorrect volumes being dispensed, resulting
in the incorrect sample or reagent concentration, which affects the outcome of experiments
(Hanahan, 1983).
4. Equipment usage: Improper operation, maintenance, or calibration of laboratory equipment
can generate unreliable or inconsistent results. For instance, inaccurate temperature settings
for incubation or heat shock can affect the transformation efficiency (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
To minimize human errors, it is essential to maintain good laboratory practices, maintaining
proper organization of the workspace, labeling samples accurately, and double-checking
reagent concentrations. Additionally, regularly calibrating and maintaining equipment,
following established protocols carefully, and incorporating appropriate controls into
experiments will help reduce the occurrence of human errors and enhance the overall success
of the genomic library construction process.

competent cell strains to improve the overall success of the genomic library construction
process (Cirino et al., 2003). Moreover, ensuring a suitable recovery time for transformed cells,
providing a nutrient-rich medium during recovery, using appropriate plating methods and
conditions, and including positive and negative controls in each transformation experiment will
aid in enhancing the efficiency of the genomic library construction and subsequent functional
selection of the streptomycin resistance-conferring rspL gene (Hanahan, 1983).

Had she forgotten the mighty storm clouds that surround our Potez 62 as we continued towards Naples, ignoring the warnings from the passengers and the yowls emitted by the fickle and gale-whipped wind? And what about the sudden gravitational onslaught, that merciless chain jerk right before things began to fade?

“You wear that suspicious look lightly nowadays,” Caroline said when my half-bushy eyebrows lifted at the mention of the word ‘crash’. “But trust me, there was no crash. Even ninety horses wouldn’t tap dance to your distress signals like this. It does, however, create the perfect setup to keep us both down for the metaphorical count.”

My eyes caught her amused smirk as her gaze drifted from me to her own body, lying in the hospital bed right across from mine.

“Strange,” she declared. “Other than this hideous cast on my arm, I feel like I just took a solid hit in one of my lost poker games, nothing more.”

“Rubbish!” My mouth disagreed, even though the curiosity brew was not stirred healthily. “It’s one thing to bounce back from a rough landing, as slim as our pretty little odds may be considering the circumstances we found ourselves in, but quite another to pretend nothing enigmatic happened.”

Caroline’s expression remained playfully grim. Perhaps intense would be the accurate term, but I would never grant her that satisfaction. "Until their motive reveals itself and crawls into broad daylight so we can watch the worm suffer its demise at the magnificent swat of our wingtips, we can have our own melodrama playing in their faces. We can do it; run our own little circus.”

“Yes,” I said, the words burning in my throat like a shot of close-to-budget-brand vodka. As my half-closed eyes began to flutter back into unconsciousness, a reluctant corner of my freshly soured ego cried, “I do reckon we’ll fly low for a while, even if I’m to put on heels just to lift my turrets.”

Caroline threw her hands in the air with mirth bubbling under the veneer of mock solemnity. “And there she lands like a deflated dirigible. Pat, your refined spirit never disappoints. Let’s rest and heal, then give our would-be administrators the flying rebuke of the century.”

She grinned like a Spitfire pilot who just spied Luftwaffe planes on the nearby tarmac. I couldn’t help but smile back at her infectious enthusiasm, even though I had to smack down the mounting nag of unattended soreness that was staging a rally inside my gut. A perfect mystery opponent deserves an unyielding champion, or so she believes, and as much as I would love to apply the breaks on her hair-brained notions, I owed it to her for hauling me out of the smoldering British monotony and retaining the exact level of adrenaline and cool-headed navigation our dangerous aerial endeavors require.

Still, one thing gnawed like the insides of a sapper’s belly: if this bizarre act was a grand rullery with consequences set at least a decade apart from grace and fume, the grand puppeteer orchestrating the whole masterful obfuscation must have a grander, sweeter and possibly deadly carrot tucked inside their sleeves. And as much as I whinged, it was devilish entertaining to think about the adventures we had coming before the ticket was finally stamped…

Buckle up, Potez 62, and bring your prettiest bucket of bolts for good luck’s sake, for this may turn out to be a flight without a leash, and perhaps even without our wicked wheels firmly hooked to the caboose. What a shame, for those Italian dinner plans vaporized just like our plane."

resistant strain of E.coli top10 (4537 bp) as the genomic DNA which will be incorporated into
puc19 plasmid (2686 bp) vector as proposed earlier in PART B proposal document.

competent cells (O.D. value = 0.77). To confirm the success of ligation the transformed product

streptomycin plates to verify the rspl gene streptomycin resistance property.

Discussion
The primary objective of this project was to create a genomic library using a streptomycinresistant strain of E.coli Top10 (4537 bp) as the genomic DNA, incorporating it into a pUC19
plasmid (2686 bp) vector (Cirino et al., 2003). The successful construction of this genomic
library was expected to confer streptomycin resistance to a recipient E.coli strain Mach1
through the functional selection of the rspL gene (Hanahan, 1983). However, throughout the
experiment, several challenges were encountered, leading to changes in the experimental
design and troubleshooting of errors.
An initial gel electrophoresis performed to confirm the presence of the rspL gene after digestion
of genomic DNA with BamHI resulted in no visible bands. This was primarily due to the low
concentration of the originally isolated genomic Top10 DNA (33.2 ng/µL), which was further
diluted during the digestion reaction and loading of the gel (Inoue et al., 1990). This
concentration was below the minimum detection limit required for the INtRON RedSafeTM
nucleic acid stain to work efficiently (50 ng/µL). As a consequence, no bands were detected,
and the experiment had to be repeated with a new and cleaned up genomic DNA sample.
Subsequent gel electrophoresis performed after digesting the cleaned-up genomic DNA with
BamHI showed successful digestion of the genomic Top10 DNA, as evidenced by a shorter
smear in comparison to the uncut band of the genomic DNA (Sorek et al., 2013). In addition, the
plasmid pUC19 showed two very faint bands after digestion with BamHI, indicating appropriate
digestion of the plasmid as well.
Part B write up 15
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
A ligation reaction was set up using a 1:1 ratio for cut genomic Top10 DNA (insert) and cut
plasmid pUC19 (vector) (Chen & Dubnau, 2004). After overnight incubation at 4 °C, the ligated
product was transformed into Mach1 chemically competent cells. The initial transformation
results were inconclusive due to contamination observed in the positive control plate.
Moreover, the second transformation attempt resulted in an unsuccessful transformation due
to inefficient uptake of DNA by the host organism, which might have been caused by several
factors, such as improper preparation of competent cells, issues concerning the ligation
reaction, or the transformation protocol itself (Inoue et al., 1990).
To increase the likelihood of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene, a third gel
electrophoresis was performed using HindIII in addition to BamHI for digesting both genomic
Top10 DNA and plasmid pUC19 (Cirino et al., 2003). The use of two different enzymes would
increase the accuracy of the construct and facilitate the incorporation of the desired fragment
into the plasmid (Hanahan, 1983).
Based on the information provided by the restriction analyzer, the BamHI enzyme cuts at two
different sites on genomic DNA (180 and 2865), producing large fragments that appeared as a
smear in the gel electrophoresis images (Sorek et al., 2013). HindIII was introduced to cut at an
additional site (4130) on genomic DNA, increasing the likelihood that the fragment containing
the rspL gene would be successfully incorporated into the plasmid (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
In summary, the construction of a genomic library using E.coli Top10 genomic DNA and pUC19
plasmid DNA encountered several challenges throughout the experiment, including low DNA
concentrations, contamination, and inefficient transformation (Inoue et al., 1990). The
introduction of the HindIII enzyme in addition to BamHI for restriction digestion was expected
to increase the probability of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene (Cirino et al., 2003).
Furthermore, troubleshooting in each area of competent cells preparation, ligation reaction,
and transformation protocol can assist in identifying and rectifying these challenges, such as reevaluating the insert-to-vector ratio, incubation time, and temperature for the ligation reaction
or testing and optimizing various transformation conditions (Hanahan, 1983).
For this experiment, the most likely problem would be with transformation. It could be
optimized and modified by making changes mentioned below:
a. Temperature and duration: Confirm that the heat shock conditions (e.g. 42°C for 30-45
seconds) are appropriate for your cells (Inoue et al., 1990).
b. Recovery duration: Allow adequate time (usually 1 hour) for the cells to recover and express
the antibiotic resistance marker (Sorek et al., 2013).
c. Optimal antibiotic concentration: Ensure the appropriate concentration of streptomycin for
selection is used on the plates. Too high or low of a concentration may result in inadequate
selection (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).

In addition to the technical challenges faced during the genomic library construction, human
errors could also have contributed to the unsuccessful or inconclusive results. These errors can
occur in sample handling, reagent preparation, equipment usage, and protocol execution. Such
errors may include:
1. Cross-contamination: During handling of samples, there is potential for cross-contamination
between different DNA samples or between the samples and reagents, leading to undesired
results (Inoue et al., 1990).
2. Reagent preparation: Errors can occur while preparing various reagents such as buffers,
enzyme solutions, or antibiotics. These could include inaccurate measurement or mixing of
components, resulting in incorrect concentrations that can affect experimental outcomes
(Sorek et al., 2013).
3. Pipetting errors: Inaccurate pipetting can lead to incorrect volumes being dispensed, resulting
in the incorrect sample or reagent concentration, which affects the outcome of experiments
(Hanahan, 1983).
4. Equipment usage: Improper operation, maintenance, or calibration of laboratory equipment
can generate unreliable or inconsistent results. For instance, inaccurate temperature settings
for incubation or heat shock can affect the transformation efficiency (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
To minimize human errors, it is essential to maintain good laboratory practices, maintaining
proper organization of the workspace, labeling samples accurately, and double-checking
reagent concentrations. Additionally, regularly calibrating and maintaining equipment,
following established protocols carefully, and incorporating appropriate controls into
experiments will help reduce the occurrence of human errors and enhance the overall success
of the genomic library construction process.
Future experiments can investigate alternative restriction enzymes, plasmid vectors, and
competent cell strains to improve the overall success of the genomic library construction
process (Cirino et al., 2003). Moreover, ensuring a suitable recovery time for transformed cells,
providing a nutrient-rich medium during recovery, using appropriate plating methods and
conditions, and including positive and negative controls in each transformation experiment will
aid in enhancing the efficiency of the genomic library construction and subsequent functional
selection of the streptomycin resistance-conferring rspL gene (Hanahan, 1983).

concentrations, contamination, and inefficient transformation. Optimization of the
transformation process, selection of alternative restriction enzymes, plasmid vectors, and
competent cell strains could enhance the overall success of the genomic library construction
and subsequent functional selection of the streptomycin resistance-conferring rspL gene.
Future experiments should also emphasize proper controls, recovery conditions, and nutrientrich media to improve the efficiency of this process.

proofread: AI systems like ChatGPT are language models trained with statistical analysis techniques. At their core, their function is to generate human-like text based on patterns learned from large text corpora. Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT are based on technologies such as the Transformer architecture and cannot be subjective, conscious, nor capable of human empathy or emotion.

LLMs use neural networks trained on “token” sequences - entities such as words or characters. The model uses probabilities to predict the most plausible continuations of the sequence of tokens. By optimizing these probability estimates, the LLM creates an illusion of coherence and understanding, even though it learns based only on statistical relationships.

In this context, it is important to emphasize that LLMs merely simulate human communication; they do not interpret, create, or understand content in the same way that humans do. Their “knowledge” is the result of identifying patterns in the data input during their training phase.

Because of these fundamental properties of AI systems like ChatGPT, which do not possess subjectivity or consciousness, regulation of AI based on the assumption of potential acquisition of subjectivity and consciousness should be reconsidered. Instead, I recommend that regulatory efforts focus on the actual functioning of these models and the potential impact of their application on society, the economy, and the environment.

To achieve appropriate and effective regulation of AI, the focus should be on specific factors such as transparency, accountability, privacy, fairness, and sustainability.

Discussion
The primary objective of this project was to create a genomic library using a streptomycinresistant strain of E.coli Top10 (4537 bp) as the genomic DNA, incorporating it into a pUC19
plasmid (2686 bp) vector (Cirino et al., 2003). The successful construction of this genomic
library was expected to confer streptomycin resistance to a recipient E.coli strain Mach1
through the functional selection of the rspL gene (Hanahan, 1983). However, throughout the
experiment, several challenges were encountered, leading to changes in the experimental
design and troubleshooting of errors.
An initial gel electrophoresis performed to confirm the presence of the rspL gene after digestion
of genomic DNA with BamHI resulted in no visible bands. This was primarily due to the low
concentration of the originally isolated genomic Top10 DNA (33.2 ng/µL), which was further
diluted during the digestion reaction and loading of the gel (Inoue et al., 1990). This
concentration was below the minimum detection limit required for the INtRON RedSafeTM
nucleic acid stain to work efficiently (50 ng/µL). As a consequence, no bands were detected,
and the experiment had to be repeated with a new and cleaned up genomic DNA sample.
Subsequent gel electrophoresis performed after digesting the cleaned-up genomic DNA with
BamHI showed successful digestion of the genomic Top10 DNA, as evidenced by a shorter
smear in comparison to the uncut band of the genomic DNA (Sorek et al., 2013). In addition, the
plasmid pUC19 showed two very faint bands after digestion with BamHI, indicating appropriate
digestion of the plasmid as well.
Part B write up 15
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
A ligation reaction was set up using a 1:1 ratio for cut genomic Top10 DNA (insert) and cut
plasmid pUC19 (vector) (Chen & Dubnau, 2004). After overnight incubation at 4 °C, the ligated
product was transformed into Mach1 chemically competent cells. The initial transformation
results were inconclusive due to contamination observed in the positive control plate.
Moreover, the second transformation attempt resulted in an unsuccessful transformation due
to inefficient uptake of DNA by the host organism, which might have been caused by several
factors, such as improper preparation of competent cells, issues concerning the ligation
reaction, or the transformation protocol itself (Inoue et al., 1990).
To increase the likelihood of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene, a third gel
electrophoresis was performed using HindIII in addition to BamHI for digesting both genomic
Top10 DNA and plasmid pUC19 (Cirino et al., 2003). The use of two different enzymes would
increase the accuracy of the construct and facilitate the incorporation of the desired fragment
into the plasmid (Hanahan, 1983).
Based on the information provided by the restriction analyzer, the BamHI enzyme cuts at two
different sites on genomic DNA (180 and 2865), producing large fragments that appeared as a
smear in the gel electrophoresis images (Sorek et al., 2013). HindIII was introduced to cut at an
additional site (4130) on genomic DNA, increasing the likelihood that the fragment containing
the rspL gene would be successfully incorporated into the plasmid (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
In summary, the construction of a genomic library using E.coli Top10 genomic DNA and pUC19
plasmid DNA encountered several challenges throughout the experiment, including low DNA
concentrations, contamination, and inefficient transformation (Inoue et al., 1990). The
introduction of the HindIII enzyme in addition to BamHI for restriction digestion was expected
to increase the probability of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene (Cirino et al., 2003).
Furthermore, troubleshooting in each area of competent cells preparation, ligation reaction,
and transformation protocol can assist in identifying and rectifying these challenges, such as reevaluating the insert-to-vector ratio, incubation time, and temperature for the ligation reaction
or testing and optimizing various transformation conditions (Hanahan, 1983).
For this experiment, the most likely problem would be with transformation. It could be
optimized and modified by making changes mentioned below:
a. Temperature and duration: Confirm that the heat shock conditions (e.g. 42°C for 30-45
seconds) are appropriate for your cells (Inoue et al., 1990).
b. Recovery duration: Allow adequate time (usually 1 hour) for the cells to recover and express
the antibiotic resistance marker (Sorek et al., 2013).
c. Optimal antibiotic concentration: Ensure the appropriate concentration of streptomycin for
selection is used on the plates. Too high or low of a concentration may result in inadequate
selection (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
Part B write up 16
Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
In addition to the technical challenges faced during the genomic library construction, human
errors could also have contributed to the unsuccessful or inconclusive results. These errors can
occur in sample handling, reagent preparation, equipment usage, and protocol execution. Such
errors may include:
1. Cross-contamination: During handling of samples, there is potential for cross-contamination
between different DNA samples or between the samples and reagents, leading to undesired
results (Inoue et al., 1990).
2. Reagent preparation: Errors can occur while preparing various reagents such as buffers,
enzyme solutions, or antibiotics. These could include inaccurate measurement or mixing of
components, resulting in incorrect concentrations that can affect experimental outcomes
(Sorek et al., 2013).
3. Pipetting errors: Inaccurate pipetting can lead to incorrect volumes being dispensed, resulting
in the incorrect sample or reagent concentration, which affects the outcome of experiments
(Hanahan, 1983).
4. Equipment usage: Improper operation, maintenance, or calibration of laboratory equipment
can generate unreliable or inconsistent results. For instance, inaccurate temperature settings
for incubation or heat shock can affect the transformation efficiency (Chen & Dubnau, 2004).
To minimize human errors, it is essential to maintain good laboratory practices, maintaining
proper organization of the workspace, labeling samples accurately, and double-checking
reagent concentrations. Additionally, regularly calibrating and maintaining equipment,
following established protocols carefully, and incorporating appropriate controls into
experiments will help reduce the occurrence of human errors and enhance the overall success
of the genomic library construction process.
Future experiments can investigate alternative restriction enzymes, plasmid vectors, and
competent cell strains to improve the overall success of the genomic library construction
process (Cirino et al., 2003). Moreover, ensuring a suitable recovery time for transformed cells,
providing a nutrient-rich medium during recovery, using appropriate plating methods and
conditions, and including positive and negative controls in each transformation experiment will
aid in enhancing the efficiency of the genomic library construction and subsequent functional
selection of the streptomycin resistance-conferring rspL gene (Hanahan, 1983).

Project Class Descriptions
1. ParkingLot Class
Description
This class is used to represent a parking lot. It contains methods for adding parking spots, parking and removing vehicles, and retrieving information about the parking lot.
Class Fields
• Int capacity: An integer representing the maximum number of parking spots in the parking lot.
• LinkedList<ParkingSpots> parkingSpots: A LinkedList of ParkingSpot objects representing the parking spots in the parking lot.
Constructors
• ParkingLot(int capacity): Creates a new ParkingLot object with the specified capacity
• ParkingLot(int capacity, int numRGSpots, int numEVSpots, int numRVSpots): Creates a new ParkingLot object with the specified capacity and number of spots for each type of vehicle. Check in place if the number of spots requested is greater than the capacity.
Methods
• addParkingSpot(String type): Adds a new parking spot to the parking lot with the specified type ("rg", "ev", or "rv"). If the capacity has been reached, it will print a message stating that the capacity has been reached.
• getCapacity(): Returns the maximum capacity of the parking lot.
• getOccupancy(): Returns the current number of parked vehicles in the parking lot.
• getSize(): Returns the current number of parking spots in the lot
• isFull(): Returns a boolean indicating whether the parking lot is currently full.
• isAtCapacity(): Returns Boolean indicating whether the number of parking spots in the lot is at capacity.
• parkVehicle(Vehicle vehicle): Parks the specified vehicle in an available parking spot of the appropriate type. If no appropriate spot is available, it will print a message stating that there is no appropriate spot available. If the parking lot is full, it will print a message stating that the parking lot is full.
• removeVehicle(Vehicle vehicle): Removes the specified vehicle from its assigned parking spot.
• parkingSpots(): Returns a LinkedList of ParkingSpot objects representing the parking spots in the parking lot, used in the SearchEngine class
• findAvailableSpot(Vehicle vehicle): Private method used to find an available parking spot of the appropriate type for the specified vehicle. If no appropriate spot is available, it will return null.
Notes
• The addParkingSpot() method will create different types of parking spots based on the type of vehicle.
• The parkVehicle() method will assign a parking spot to the specified vehicle and update the parkingSpot field of the vehicle object.
• The removeVehicle() method will remove the vehicle from its assigned parking spot and set the parkingSpot field of the vehicle object to null.
• The findAvailableSpot() method is used by the parkVehicle() method to find an available parking spot for the specified vehicle.
2. ParkingSpot Class
Description
The ParkingSpot class provides a blueprint for creating parking spots for vehicles. It contains fields to store information about the spot's ID, type, and whether it is free or occupied by a vehicle. It also has methods to assign and remove vehicles, calculate parking fees, and validate spot types.
Class Fields
• int id: assigns an ID number to the parking spot
• String spotType: specifies the type of parking spot (regular, electric, or RV)
• Vehicle vehicle: the vehicle currently parked in this spot
• Boolean isFree: indicates whether the spot is free to be assigned to a vehicle
• LocalDateTime entryTime: the time when the vehicle was parked in the spot, used to calculate parking fee
Constructors
• ParkingSpot(int id, String type): constructs a new ParkingSpot object with the specified ID and type. Check in place if an invalid spot type is provided.
Methods
• getId() : int: returns the ID of the parking spot
• getSpotType() : String: returns the type of parking spot (regular, electric, or RV)
• getVehicle() : Vehicle: returns the vehicle parked in this spot
• isFree() : boolean: returns true if the spot is free, false if it is occupied by a vehicle
• assignVehicle(Vehicle vehicle) : void: assigns the specified vehicle to this spot if it is free. If the spot is already occupied, throws an IllegalArgumentException
• removeVehicle() : void: removes the vehicle from the spot, calculates the parking fee and prints it to the console. Check in place if the spot is already free.
• parkingFee() : double: calculates the parking fee based on the spot type and duration of parking. Check in place if the spot is free.
• isValidVehicleType(String type) : boolean: checks whether the provided spot type is valid (regular, electric, or RV)
Notes
• Parking fees are calculated based on the spot type and duration of parking. The base rate is $3, with additional charges of $15/hour for regular spots, $21/hour for electric spots, and $30/hour for RV spots.
• The assignVehicle method also sets the parking spot of the assigned vehicle to this spot.
3. Vehicle Class
Description
The Vehicle class represents a vehicle that can be parked in a parking spot. It has fields for the vehicle's brand, model, license plate, type, and a formatted string with information about the vehicle. It also has a reference to the parking spot where it is currently parked.
Class Fields
• String brand: a string representing the vehicle's brand
• String model: a string representing the vehicle's model
• String licencePlate: a string representing the vehicle's license plate
• String type: a string representing the vehicle's type (regular, electric, or RV)
• String info: a formatted string containing information about the vehicle
• ParkingSpot parkingSpot: a reference to the parking spot where the vehicle is parked
Constructors
• Vehicle(String carBrand, String carModel, String licencePlate, String type): constructs a new Vehicle object with the given brand, model, license plate, and type. Check in place if the type is invalid.
Methods
• getBrand(): returns the vehicle's brand.
• getModel(): returns the vehicle's model.
• getLicencePlate(): returns the vehicle's license plate.
• getType(): returns the vehicle's type (regular, electric, or RV).
• getParkingSpot(): returns the parking spot where the vehicle is parked.
• setParkingSpot(ParkingSpot parkingSpot): sets the parking spot where the vehicle is parked.
• getInfo(): returns a formatted string with information about the vehicle (brand, model, type, and license plate).
• isValidVehicleType(String type): returns true if the given type is valid (regular, electric, or RV), and false otherwise.
Notes
• The Vehicle class is used in conjunction with the ParkingSpot class to create a parking management system. A Vehicle is assigned to a ParkingSpot when it is parked, and the parking fee is calculated based on the time the Vehicle was parked in the ParkingSpot.
4. SearchEngine Class
Description
The SearchEngine class provides facility to search for vehicles currently parked in the lot it is assigned to, based on brand, type and licence plate.
Class Fields
• LinkedList<ParkingSpot> parkingSpots: A LinkedList of ParkingSpot objects representing the parking spots in the parking lot.
• ParkingLot parkinglot: Assigning a ParkingLot object to the search engine.
Constructors
• SearchEngine(ParkingLot parkingLot): constructs a new SearchEngine object with a parking lot assigned to it.
Methods
• searchByBrand(String carBrand): Looks up Vehicles currently parked in the parking lot of a particular brand.
• searchByType(String carType): Looks up Vehicles currently parked in the parking lot of a particular type (rg, ev, rv).
• searchByPlate(String carBrand): Looks up Vehicle currently parked in the parking lot of a particular Licence Plate.
• updateLL(): Updates internal copy of parking lot’s list, to have the most recent version for a check.

Jetul and Japneet April 9, 2023
