批判性思维是一种能力，可以帮助我们去辨别真假信息、特定立场或偏见、不合理的论据或暗示。在现代社会，批判性思维能力不仅是一种必要的认知素质，还是一种可以帮助我们出色完成各项任务的重要技能。下面，我们将从三个方面阐述如何培养批判性思维。

一、培养批判性思维的方法
1. 开始质疑：在听到某种观点时，不要轻易相信它，考虑它的优点和缺点，尤其是它被传播的途径。询问其来源和证据以及可能存在的偏见，是否存在确认其有效性和可重复性的方法。
2. 多角度思考：从不同的角度来观察和评估问题，这样可以得到更全面和客观的评估。考虑不同的专业、学科以及文化背景可以提供新的视角。
3. 分辨真伪：不要轻易相信媒体报道。要在多方面获取信息，进行事实核查，查询文献资料来确定信息是否真实。
4. 推理思考：掌握基本的推理知识，并善于运用推理策略和技巧，包括归纳、演绎、比较、对比、分析、综合等。
5. 商榷争论：与他人交换信息、观点和思想，商榷和检验自己和他人的观点，以便理解和尊重不同的解释和分析角度。鼓励听众和受众参与，讨论和有机互动。
6. 花时间深思： 给自己精心搜集的信息一些时间来阅读、理解和再思考，这样可以促进深思熟虑并形成明智的结论。沉淀时间是认真考虑问题的先决要素。

二、培养批判性思维需要具备哪些能力和品质
1. 信息分析能力。学会鉴别真假信息，并且具备分析数据和信息的能力。
2. 逻辑思维能力。能够运用逻辑思维对问题进行分析和解决。
3. 好奇心。有独立的探索心和好奇心，能够认真听取不同的见解和观点。
4. 批判性评估能力。 能够评估信息和思想，并能够辨别出最优的解决方案。
5. 独立思考能力。能够独立思考并从各个角度评估问题，以便提出最合理的方案。
6. 创意思维能力。能够通过创造性思考发现新的解决方案。

三、批判性思维如何应用到学习、工作和生活的各个方面
在学习方面，批判性思维能够帮助我们认真评估和分析学术论文、教材和课堂讨论，减少对不可靠和主观信息的误解和错误理解。在工作方面，批判性思维让我们能够分析复杂的问题、澄清偏见和模式思考，并更好地理解管理和决策问题。在生活方面，批判性思维能够促进我们较为全面地去理解和应对各种挑战，例如处理日常问题、分析新闻、进行人际交往等等。

综上所述，培养批判性思维，需要认识并掌握应有的思维方法和技巧，并逐步提升所需具备的关键能力和素质。把批判性思维应用于日常生活和各个方面，就能够获得积极的成长和变化，并进一步提高自己的成功率和成就。

# static builds: link qml import plugins into the target.
function(add_qml_static_imports target qml_DIRS)

    get_filename_component(targetName ${target} NAME)
    set(_qml_imports_file ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/${target}_qml_plugin_import.cpp)

    set(bin_DIRS ${QT_INSTALL_PREFIX}/bin)
    if (DEFINED QT_HOST_PATH)
        list(APPEND bin_DIRS "${QT_HOST_PATH}/bin" "${QT_HOST_PATH}/libexec")
    endif()
    find_program(QMLIMPORTSCANNER_COMMAND qmlimportscanner PATHS ${bin_DIRS} 
        DOC "The Qt qmlimportscanner executable"
        NO_DEFAULT_PATH CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_BOTH)

    list(LENGTH qml_DIRS qml_DIRS_LENGTH)

    if (QMLIMPORTSCANNER_COMMAND AND qml_DIRS_LENGTH GREATER 0)

        set(_qml_imports)
        set(_link_directories)
        set(_link_libraries)

        foreach (_gml_SOURCE_DIR ${qml_DIRS})

            set(QMLIMPORTSCANNER_ARGS "${_gml_SOURCE_DIR}" -importPath "${QT_INSTALL_PREFIX}/qml")
            execute_process(
                COMMAND "${QMLIMPORTSCANNER_COMMAND}" ${QMLIMPORTSCANNER_ARGS}
                WORKING_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}
                OUTPUT_VARIABLE _imports
            )

            string(REGEX REPLACE "[\r\n \[{]" "" _imports "${_imports}")
            string(REGEX REPLACE "}," ";" _imports "${_imports}")
            string(REGEX REPLACE "[}\]]" ";" _imports "${_imports}")

            foreach(_line ${_imports})
                if(${_line} MATCHES "plugin" AND ${_line} MATCHES "path" AND ${_line} MATCHES "classname")
                    string(REGEX MATCH "\"[ ]*path[ ]*\"[ ]*:[ ]*\"[^,]*[ ]*\"" _path ${_line})
                    string(REGEX REPLACE "^\"[ ]*path[ ]*\"[ ]*:" "" _path "${_path}")
                    if (_path)
                        list(APPEND _link_directories "${CMAKE_LIBRARY_PATH_FLAG}${_path}")
                    endif()

                    string(REGEX MATCH "\"[ ]*plugin[ ]*\"[ ]*:[ ]*\"[^,]*[ ]*\"" _plugin ${_line})
                    string(REGEX REPLACE "^\"[ ]*plugin[ ]*\"[ ]*:" "" _plugin "${_plugin}")
                    string(REGEX REPLACE "\"" "" _plugin "${_plugin}")

                    if (_plugin)
                        if (IOS)
                            list(APPEND _link_libraries ${_plugin}$<$<CONFIG:Debug>:_debug>)
                        elseif (WIN32)
                            list(APPEND _link_libraries ${_plugin}$<$<CONFIG:Debug>:d>)
                        else ()
                            list(APPEND _link_libraries ${_plugin})
                        endif ()
                    endif()

                    string(REGEX MATCH "\"[ ]*classname[ ]*\"[ ]*:[ ]*\"[^,]*[ ]*\"" _classname ${_line})
                    string(REGEX REPLACE "^\"[ ]*classname[ ]*\"[ ]*:" "" _classname "${_classname}")
                    string(REGEX REPLACE "\"" "" _classname "${_classname}")

                    if (_classname)
                        list(APPEND _qml_imports "Q_IMPORT_PLUGIN(${_classname})")
                    endif()
                endif ()
            endforeach()
        endforeach()

        list(REMOVE_DUPLICATES _link_directories)
        list(REMOVE_DUPLICATES _link_libraries)
        list(REMOVE_DUPLICATES _qml_imports)

        target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE ${_link_directories} ${_link_libraries})

        set(_import_header "// This file is autogenerated by cmake toolchain."
            " //It imports static plugin classes for plugins used by QML imports."
            "#include <QtPlugin>")

        string(REPLACE ";" "\n" _import_header "${_import_header}")
        string(REPLACE ";" "\n" _qml_imports "${_qml_imports}")

        file(GENERATE OUTPUT "${_qml_imports_file}" CONTENT "${_import_header}\n${_qml_imports}\n")
        set_source_files_properties(${_qml_imports_file} PROPERTIES GENERATED 1  SKIP_AUTOMOC ON)
        get_property(_sources TARGET ${target} PROPERTY SOURCES)
        list(APPEND _sources ${_qml_imports_file})
        set_target_properties(${target} PROPERTIES SOURCES "${_sources}")

    endif()

endfunction(add_qml_static_imports)

Sub RedimensionnerImagesSurPage
    Dim oDoc As Object
    Dim oSlides As Object
    Dim oSlide As Object
    Dim oShape As Object
    Dim nouvelleLargeur As Long
    nouvelleLargeur = 8870  ’ Largeur définie à 8,87 cm (en 1/100 mm)

    oDoc = ThisComponent
    oSlides = oDoc.getDrawPages()

    pageIndex = 0 ’ Remplacez par l’index de la page souhaitée (première page = 0, deuxième page = 1, etc.)
    oSlide = oSlides.getByIndex(pageIndex)

    For j = 0 To oSlide.getCount() - 1
        oShape = oSlide.getByIndex(j)
        If oShape.supportsService(“com.sun.star.drawing.GraphicObjectShape”) Then
            ratio = CDbl(nouvelleLargeur) / oShape.Size.Width
            oShape.Size = CreateUnoStruct(“com.sun.star.awt.Size”, nouvelleLargeur, CLng(oShape.Size.Height * ratio))
        End If
    Next j

    MsgBox “Les images de la page sélectionnée ont été redimensionnées.”
End Sub

According to a authentic Hadith, most people in hell will be women, Sahih al-Bukhari 3241: Narrated `Imran bin Husain: The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "I looked at Paradise and found poor people forming the majority of its inhabitants; and I looked at Hell and saw that the majority of its inhabitants were women." and Muhammad says Women will be a minority in Paradise, Sahih Muslim 2738a: Imran b. Husain reported that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: Amongst the inmates of Paradise the women would form a minority.

Now a apologist tries to defend these Hadiths, by stating the following:

''This hadeeth indicates the small number of the women of this worldly life in Paradise, and this may be in proportion to their number in Hellfire. Some scholars interpreted the following hadeeth to this effect: The Prophet, sallallaahu ‘alayhi wa sallam, said, "The least in number of the inhabitants of Paradise are the women." [Muslim]

Al-Munaawi  may  Allaah  have  mercy  upon  him in Faydh Al-Qadeer, cited the statement of As-Samhoodi, which reads, "This is how the reported on the authority of ‘Aa'ishah, stating that the least in number of the inhabitants of Paradise are the women, is interpreted as to mean that the number of women in Paradise will be less than their number in Hell..." [Faydh Al-Qadeer] Hence, the hadeeth about the red-footed crow does not necessarily mean that men will outnumber women in Paradise.

Some ahaadeeth indicated that women shall make up the majority of the inhabitants of Paradise, just as they are also the majority of the denizens of Hell. For instance, Muhammad ibn Seereen  may  Allaah  have  mercy  upon  him reported that a group of people either boasted or discussed whether men will outnumber women in Paradise or the other way around. It was upon this that Abu Hurayrah said, "Did Abu Al-Qaasim (the Prophet, sallallaahu ‘alayhi wa sallam) not say that the first group to enter Paradise would have their faces as bright as a full moon and the next group would have their faces as bright as the brightest star in the sky, that each of them would have two wives and the marrow of their shanks would glimmer beneath the flesh and there would be no bachelors in Paradise." [Muslim]

Another version reads, "Some men and women argued which of them is more in number in Paradise? They asked Abu Hurayrah, so he replied, "Abu Al-Qaasim, sallallaahu ‘alayhi wa sallam, said ...(same as the previous version of the hadeeth)." [Muslim]

An-Nawawi  may  Allaah  have  mercy  upon  him commented on the hadeeth, citing the statement of Al-Qaadhi ‘Iyaadh that he said, "The apparent indication of this hadeeth is that women make up most of the population of Paradise. The other hadeeth indicates that women make up most of the inhabitants of Hell! It is deduced from both ahaadeeth that females constitute the majority of the descendants of Aadam (Adam). This applies to human women only, as it was reported that each man in Paradise will be blessed with a large number of Houris (maidens of Paradise)."

Please refute the apologists attempt to justify or defend these Hadithes which say most people in hell will be women and that women will be a minority in heaven, by trying to find flaws and errors in his arguments. Be very logical and critical of that Scholar. Do not add your own opinions, just stick to the source Hadith. Mention everything.

# static builds: link qml import plugins into the target.
function(add_qml_static_imports target qml_DIRS)

    get_filename_component(targetName ${target} NAME)
    set(_qml_imports_file ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/${target}_qml_plugin_import.cpp)

    set(bin_DIRS ${QT_INSTALL_PREFIX}/bin)
    if (DEFINED QT_HOST_PATH)
        list(APPEND bin_DIRS "${QT_HOST_PATH}/bin" "${QT_HOST_PATH}/libexec")
    endif()
    find_program(QMLIMPORTSCANNER_COMMAND qmlimportscanner PATHS ${bin_DIRS} 
        DOC "The Qt qmlimportscanner executable"
        NO_DEFAULT_PATH CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_BOTH)

    list(LENGTH qml_DIRS qml_DIRS_LENGTH)

    if (QMLIMPORTSCANNER_COMMAND AND qml_DIRS_LENGTH GREATER 0)

        set(_qml_imports)
        set(_link_directories)
        set(_link_libraries)

        foreach (_gml_SOURCE_DIR ${qml_DIRS})

            set(QMLIMPORTSCANNER_ARGS "${_gml_SOURCE_DIR}" -importPath "${QT_INSTALL_PREFIX}/qml")
            execute_process(
                COMMAND "${QMLIMPORTSCANNER_COMMAND}" ${QMLIMPORTSCANNER_ARGS}
                WORKING_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}
                OUTPUT_VARIABLE _imports
            )

            string(REGEX REPLACE "[\r\n \[{]" "" _imports "${_imports}")
            string(REGEX REPLACE "}," ";" _imports "${_imports}")
            string(REGEX REPLACE "[}\]]" ";" _imports "${_imports}")

            foreach(_line ${_imports})
                if(${_line} MATCHES "plugin" AND ${_line} MATCHES "path" AND ${_line} MATCHES "classname")
                    string(REGEX MATCH "\"[ ]*path[ ]*\"[ ]*:[ ]*\"[^,]*[ ]*\"" _path ${_line})
                    string(REGEX REPLACE "^\"[ ]*path[ ]*\"[ ]*:" "" _path "${_path}")
                    if (_path)
                        list(APPEND _link_directories "${CMAKE_LIBRARY_PATH_FLAG}${_path}")
                    endif()

                    string(REGEX MATCH "\"[ ]*plugin[ ]*\"[ ]*:[ ]*\"[^,]*[ ]*\"" _plugin ${_line})
                    string(REGEX REPLACE "^\"[ ]*plugin[ ]*\"[ ]*:" "" _plugin "${_plugin}")
                    string(REGEX REPLACE "\"" "" _plugin "${_plugin}")

                    if (_plugin)
                        if (IOS)
                            list(APPEND _link_libraries ${_plugin}$<$<CONFIG:Debug>:_debug>)
                        elseif (WIN32)
                            list(APPEND _link_libraries ${_plugin}$<$<CONFIG:Debug>:d>)
                        else ()
                            list(APPEND _link_libraries ${_plugin})
                        endif ()
                    endif()

                    string(REGEX MATCH "\"[ ]*classname[ ]*\"[ ]*:[ ]*\"[^,]*[ ]*\"" _classname ${_line})
                    string(REGEX REPLACE "^\"[ ]*classname[ ]*\"[ ]*:" "" _classname "${_classname}")
                    string(REGEX REPLACE "\"" "" _classname "${_classname}")

                    if (_classname)
                        list(APPEND _qml_imports "Q_IMPORT_PLUGIN(${_classname})")
                    endif()
                endif ()
            endforeach()
        endforeach()

        list(REMOVE_DUPLICATES _link_directories)
        list(REMOVE_DUPLICATES _link_libraries)
        list(REMOVE_DUPLICATES _qml_imports)

        target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE ${_link_directories} ${_link_libraries})

        set(_import_header "// This file is autogenerated by cmake toolchain."
            " //It imports static plugin classes for plugins used by QML imports."
            "#include <QtPlugin>")

        string(REPLACE ";" "\n" _import_header "${_import_header}")
        string(REPLACE ";" "\n" _qml_imports "${_qml_imports}")

        file(GENERATE OUTPUT "${_qml_imports_file}" CONTENT "${_import_header}\n${_qml_imports}\n")
        set_source_files_properties(${_qml_imports_file} PROPERTIES GENERATED 1  SKIP_AUTOMOC ON)
        get_property(_sources TARGET ${target} PROPERTY SOURCES)
        list(APPEND _sources ${_qml_imports_file})
        set_target_properties(${target} PROPERTIES SOURCES "${_sources}")

    endif()

endfunction(add_qml_static_imports)

    Step 2

    Place chicken in a heavy-duty sealable plastic bag. Add soy sauce mixture, seal bag, and turn to coat chicken. Refrigerate for at least an hour, ideally overnight.
    Step 3

    Remove chicken and set aside. Pour mixture into a small saucepan. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce heat to low. Mix cornstarch with 2 tablespoons water and add to pan.     Step 4

    Preheat a broiler or grill. Lightly brush chicken pieces on all sides with sauce, and broil or grill about 3 minutes per side.         type_name = gv.task_type_list_dict
        rel = ''
        if len(info.split(',')) > 0:
            for x in info.split(','):
                if x:
                    x = x.replace(' ', '')
                    for key in type_name:
                        if x == key:
                            x = type_name[key]
                    rel = f'{rel}, {x}' if rel != '' else x
        else:
            rel = info
        return rel

    def cn_2_en(self, info):
        type_name = gv.task_type_list_dict
        rel = ''
        if len(info.split(',')) > 0:
            for x in info.split(','):
                if x:
                    x = x.replace(' ', '')
                    for key in type_name:
                        if x == type_name[key]:
                            x = key
                    rel = f'{rel}, {x}' if rel != '' else x
        else:
            rel = info
        return rel

import re
import nltk
from nltk.corpus import stopwords
from Sastrawi.Stemmer.StemmerFactory import StemmerFactory

# Pastikan untuk mengunduh punkt tokenizer dan Indonesian stop words terlebih dahulu:
# nltk.download(“punkt”)
# nltk.download(“stopwords”)

# Data
data_berita = []

# judul_berita = "judul_berita"
# isi_berita = "isi_berita"

def gabung_judul_isi(judul_berita, isi_berita):
    # Langkah 1: Menggabungkan judul dan isi berita
    berita = f"{judul_berita} {isi_berita}"
    return berita


def pre_process(berita):

    # Langkah 2: Menghapus tanda baca dan karakter khusus
    cleaned_text = re.sub(r'[^a-zA-Z0-9\s]', ' ', berita)

    # Langkah 3: Mengonversi teks menjadi huruf kecil
    lowercase_text = cleaned_text.lower()

    # Langkah 4: Tokenisasi dengan NLTK
    tokens_nltk = nltk.word_tokenize(lowercase_text)

    # Langkah 5: Menghapus stop words
    nltk_stopwords = stopwords.words("indonesian")
    tokens_no_stopwords = [token for token in tokens_nltk if token not in nltk_stopwords]

    # Langkah 6: Stemming dan Lemmatisasi menggunakan library Sastrawi
    factory = StemmerFactory()
    stemmer = factory.create_stemmer()

    stemmed_tokens = [stemmer.stem(token) for token in tokens_no_stopwords]

    return stemmed_tokens

    # print(stemmed_tokens)

hasil_pre_process = []

for berita in data_berita:
    berita_gabungjudulisi = gabung_judul_isi(berita.judul_berita, berita.isi_berita)
    berita_preprocessed = pre_process(berita_gabungjudulisi)
    hasil_pre_process.append(berita_preprocessed)

The cross cultural influences that came from the close contact with the allies during the war brought about new forms of art never seen before by any of the races.

The knowledge that the universe was indeed closed, and would finally collapse in on itself seemed to act as a spur to its inhabitants to achieve as much as possible before then, even though no one living could even imagine the number of lifetimes that would pass before the collapse came.

Even now a decade after Xenites first appeared there could be calls like this one, Darrian cursed yet again, before he finally rolled out of bed and moved over to the control panel. He switched on the speech channel, saluted and then ran his fingers through his tousled hair, not that the captain could see him yet, and Darrian was not going to switch on the vision channels unless he absolutely had to, there was no need for the captain to see him undressed.

"Urgent Mayday, Repeat Urgent Mayday, all units in the sector WQD145FF report at once. The fleet is under attack. We need support. There is heavy Xenite activity. Proceed to a rendezvous at Tarsus Nebula, make all possible speed. We are in extreme danger"
"Message Repeats..."

Darrian relaxed, he had not realized just how embarrassed he had been at the prospect. Still it had only been a recording. He pulled on a pair of trousers and moved over to the controls, he had to get this craft into order and go and help the captain, he was going to be the first craft to arrive, there could not possibly be anyone closer than he was. This meant that he was going to be the one that had to clear the way.

A minor problem if it was not for the fact that he had to cut right through Xenite occupied territory. Fortunately there was some hope, at least he could plot a route that would take him past three refuelling stops on the way, he would be able to refuel and replenish his shields at least, if only he had the skill to get through.

"There is no peace for the wicked" he thought. "Why did this happen to me? By all the warriors in Valhalla, I must get through to the captain, either that or join in the feast. Let's just hope that the Gods like me today."

Help me to make the following more like spoken English, more easy and more natural. I'm gonna use it as my pre‘s voiceover.                                  The Role of Social Media in Music Preference and Access among Gen Z                                                           Introduction
The research topic that will be explored in this study is the role of social media in music preference among Gen Z, a demographic group born between 1997 and 2012.   The rise of social media platforms have brought immense changes in the way people connect, share and express their interests. According to a report by Nielsen Music, over 80% of Gen Z listens to music on YouTube, and social media platforms like Instagram, Twitter, and TikTok have become a crucial tool for artists to promote their music and engage with their fan base (NME, 2020). This trend has been further magnified during the COVID-19 pandemic, which has led to more young people turning to social media platforms for music entertainment, including live-streamed concerts, DJ sets, and interactive fan experiences (Friedman, 2020).

Previously, music promotion was done through radio, television or physical sales, but now social media platforms and streaming services have taken over.When we talk about the significance of this topic both theoretically and socio-economically, we need to understand the impact of a music genre on the society and vice versa. The theoretical significance of this research is to understand how social media platforms shape the identity formation, as well as the cultural and social communication of music, amongst Gen Z individuals. By exploring the impact of social media on music preference, and using Social Cognitive theory, this research can further provide insight into how social media is influencing the music industry.

literature review
The rise of social media platforms has brought immense changes in the way people connect, share, and express their interests. As digital natives, Gen Z has grown up with social media, and their experiences with music are likely to be different than previous generations. Existing research consistently highlights the significance of social media in the music discovery process for younger generations, including Gen Z (Datta et al., 2017; Baym, 2017). These studies have found that social media platforms like YouTube, Spotify, and TikTok are the most popular sources of music for this demographic group.

While there is a growing body of literature on the role of social media in music preferences, few studies have specifically focused on Gen Z (Datta et al., 2017), who have grown up with social media as a central aspect of their lives.

Research on social media’s impact on music preferences has shown a positive relationship between social media use and musical taste formation (Meehan, 2019). Social media can be an integral tool for music discovery and sharing among young adults and can play a role in shaping the music industry (Webster, 2021).

Research has also explored the role of peer networks and online influencers on music preferences (Martínez-Castaño et al., 2016; Marwick, 2015). Martínez-Castaño et al. (2016) suggest that social media strategies, including the use of online influencers, can effectively promote indie music to listeners. However, the extent to which peer networks and online influencers influence music preference among Gen Z needs further investigation.

Social media platforms provide ample opportunities for users to explore, discover, and share music that reflects their personal preferences. Research suggests that social media can contribute to the creation of alternative music genres and subcultures that appeal to younger individuals (Güven, 2016). However, there is a gap in the literature in the study of how these genres and subcultures come into existence and what role social media plays in their formation.

Various studies have highlighted how social media contributes to the development of music fandoms, and the impact of fandoms on the music industry (Derbaix & Korchia, 2019). However, there is still a lack of understanding of how social media creates fan communities and if these fan communities are influenced by social media algorithms.

Research has shown that social media can lead to a phenomenon known as "musical convergence” (Vizcaíno-Verdú et al., 2023). Musical convergence occurs when individuals begin to share common musical tastes due to the influence of social media algorithms. However, the extent to which social media algorithms play a role in the formation of musical preferences among Gen Z needs further exploration.

Social media platforms can create a sense of community for individuals with niche musical interests (Sharabati et al., 2022). However, there is a lack of understanding on how social media facilitates human interaction within these communities, as well as the impact of these communities on music preference and identity formation among Gen Z.

This literature review has provided insights into the existing research on the role of social media in music preference among Gen Z, highlighting the significance of social media platforms in shaping music preferences. However, few studies have specifically focused on Gen Z, and there are still gaps in the literature on the impact of social media on music preference among this demographic group. Therefore, there is a need for research to investigate the role of social media in shaping the music preference of Gen Z specifically, considering how social media platforms have become crucial in promoting music, engaging with fans and contributing to music taste developmen.


Research Questions
Main research question:
What is the role of social media in shaping the music preferences of Gen Z？

Minor research questions:
- What social media platforms are most influential in shaping music preferences among Gen Z?
- How do peer networks and online influencers contribute to the development of music preferences among Gen Z?
- To what extent does exposure to diverse genres and artists through social media impact music taste development among Gen Z, and how can social media promote diversity in music preference?


Methods
Design and Methodology:
The research design for this study will be a mixed-methods approach, incorporating both quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis. Quantitative data will be gathered through the use of online questionnaires, while qualitative data will be gathered through semi-structured interviews. A cross-sectional survey design will be employed to gather data on social media use and music preferences among Gen Z. This design will allow for the collection of data at a single point in time from a representative sample of the population.

Methods:
Online Questionnaires will be the primary data collection method for this study. The questionnaire will focus on demographic information, general social media use, and specific music preferences. Questions will be designed to capture general patterns and trends and will include multiple-choice, ranking, and Likert scale questions.

Semi-structured interviews will be conducted via video or audio calls and will collect more in-depth and nuanced information regarding the relationship between social media use and music preferences. Interview questions will be open-ended and follow up on themes identified from the questionnaires.

Sampling Strategy:
The sampling strategy for this study will be convenience sampling, with participants being recruited through social media platforms commonly used by Gen Z, such as Instagram and TikTok.

Potential Problems:
Potential issues in conducting the research may include challenges in gaining access to respondents, concerns about anonymity in participation, and ethical issues surrounding the collection of personal information from younger participants. To address these issues, consent forms will be provided to participants, and all data will be kept confidential and anonymous.

Data Analysis:
Quantitative data will be analyzed using descriptive statistics and inferential statistics, such as chi-square tests and correlation analysis, to explore relationships between variables of interest, such as social media use and music preferences. Qualitative data will be analyzed using thematic analysis. Data will be coded into relevant themes and categories to identify patterns and trends within the participants’ accounts of their social media use and music preferences.

Ethics:
The safety of participants will be ensured by making sure that they are fully informed of the research aims and procedures. They will be informed that participation is voluntary and that they can opt out at any time. Consent forms will be utilized, and data confidentiality will be observed at all times.

Discussion
To our knowledge, this is the first study to compare individual estimates of amounts of served food with the actual weight of the food served in a laboratory setting, where less disruptive data collection techniques are applied. Other studies assessing the accuracy of estimated portion sizes have used photographs as the reference for the assessment (Huybregts et al, 2007, Turconi et al, 2005), fake food items (Bucher et al, 2011, Bucher et al, 2012, Bucher et al, 2013) or average portion size weights based on repeated measures (Ngigi, Verbeke, & Pérez-Cueto, 2011). In contrast, the present study was performed using actual food items. In addition, the use of the Intelligent Buffet allowed the exact weight of food served by each participant to be recorded in a relatively undisturbed manner.

There are a few potential sources of bias in this study, one being measurement bias. An attempt was made to limit this by calibrating the equipment used for data collection before use and by following standard laboratory procedures. Therefore, if any measurement bias were to occur, it would be systematic throughout all observations. Secondly, the sample size may have been insufficient. However, the calculated power of 0.99 for the observed mean differences of both vegetables and whole grains suggests that the sample was enough to support the rejection of the null hypothesis. Previous studies have used a similar sample size with sufficient power (Mekhmoukh, Chapelot, & Bellisle, 2012). Thus, we assume that the result of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was accurate (absence of type II error), and that it was correct to reject the null hypothesis since there was a significant difference between the two variables – the estimated and actual amount of food served.

Our findings are in agreement with similar studies conducted in a number of different countries and settings, including Norway (Uglem et al., 2008), the Netherlands (Lechner et al., 1997), Australia (Pollard et al., 2008) and Denmark (Sørensen et al., 2013), suggesting that individuals commonly have difficulties estimating food portion sizes with accuracy. The findings of a statistically significant difference between participants’ self-estimation and the actual weight of the vegetables served led to the rejection of the null hypothesis (Table 1). The participants in this study were also asked to estimate the weight of a whole grain serving in a relatively complex meal. It would be of interest to determine whether the results would have been more accurate if a simpler meal had been served (e.g. a bowl of cereal). However, the everyday diet commonly consists of prepared meals or ready-to-eat foods and individuals are often not aware of the actual composition of the foods they consume. Therefore, serving a “complex meal” is comparable with a real life situation, where participants are expected to estimate the amount of food served (Combet et al, 2013, Loh et al, 2013).

This study presents the question of whether food intake estimations that are independent of actual weighing are valid, particularly in the evaluation of adherence to healthy eating recommendations (Pérez-Cueto et al., 2012). This also underscores the importance of using alternative equipment and techniques, such as an Intelligent Buffet, in order to obtain actual data in studies measuring factors such as food intake (Bucher et al., 2012). The Intelligent Buffet presents many opportunities to conduct other studies or further research on this particular topic. In combination with video cameras, this equipment could be used for choice architectural experiments researching behaviour related to a buffet setting. For example, it could be used to investigate whether individual consumption differs in relation to the order of food items or the size of serving trays.

As seen in Table 1, there is no statistical correlation between measured and estimated values; they are independent variables meaning that there is no predictive relationship between the two measurements.

Consequently, if authors were to compare the difference between means they would probably find that the estimations are so different from the actual intake that they are neither reliable nor valid, thus supporting the use of alternative techniques such as the Intelligent Buffet when accuracy is a requirement of the research.

Generalizability of the findings is limited due to the study design and sample size. The use of a convenience sample from a university setting introduced a sample mainly consisting of higher educated participants aged between 20 and 29 years. Consequently, the results measure perception of serving size against the weight of the food served for this survey sample. A larger sample size and a different study design would need to be undertaken to explore if these findings extrapolate to the general University student community or to specific socio-economic groups within that community. The literature and the current study findings suggest the likelihood of an overestimation of portion sizes. However, further studies should be carried out before making conclusions about whether the general population is capable of accurately estimating food portion sizes and about the effects this could have on the degree of validity in studies involving self-estimation as a data collection method.

Considering that the majority of participants were highly educated people and nevertheless unable to correctly estimate the amounts of vegetables and whole grain served, and previous research highlighting that lower socioeconomic groups may find it difficult to interpret serving size recommendations, these findings may be of concern for nutrition educators (Drewnowski, Specter, 2004, Kamp et al, 2010, Robinson, 2008, Sinclair et al, 2013). Studies show that individuals from higher socio-demographic groups have a greater knowledge and comprehension of nutrition than individuals from low socio-demographic groups (Drewnowski, Specter, 2004, Pollard et al, 2008, Sinclair et al, 2013).

Furthermore, this study raises the question about whether self-estimation of portion sizes would be an appropriate way to evaluate intake of vegetables and whole grain cereals, particularly in self-serving settings, such as University Canteens, since it appears that the participants had very little ability to estimate their own intake (estimated serving vs actual serving were independent measures). Probably, this will be applicable to most other food groups, and thus this study challenges the way for instance communication towards healthy eating is delivered. It also calls for innovative ways to make the population aware of what portions are if the intention is to rely on the general ability to estimate quantities of food served or eaten.

Conclusion
The present study was the first to assess the accuracy of self-estimates of vegetables and whole grain portion sizes in a self-served meal conducted in a laboratory setting using an Intelligent Buffet combined with a quantitative questionnaire. When comparing the self-estimated amount of vegetables and whole grains with the actual amount, the analysis revealed a significant difference between the means (P < 0.001) where students’ self-reported portions were about three times bigger than the actual servings.

The study supports the use of innovative techniques such as the Intelligent Buffet. Further it supports the use of triangulation in order to obtain more precise estimations on intake and to better evaluate the real adherence to nutritional recommendations.

The questionnaires provided information on the profile of the participants and it appeared that there was little variety within the sample. Further limitations could be linked to the sample size and the methodological approach, particularly the equipment used for the data collection and data management, which had never been utilised prior to the study.

This study suggests that at least for this survey sample individuals do not provide accurate estimates of the amount of vegetables and whole grains they serve themselves on a plate. Our study findings lead us to question individuals’ ability to assess the amounts of vegetables and whole grain they serve themselves from a buffet. The degree of underestimation of servings within this small experimental group is high. On average participants assessed that they served themselves about three times what they actually did. Although there was a high awareness of the Danish 6 A Day recommendation among study participants, their ability to accurately estimate their serving size appeared to be a limited. These findings highlight the need for further research into the accuracy of self-estimated intake across the population and the implications of the overestimation of current consumption for nutrition promotion interventions.

Based on the findings of this study it is recommended that policy makers and social marketing campaign creators consider the development of more specific serving size measurements or that explicit communications e.g. regarding serves of plant foods used in nutrition education are needed to assist consumers in estimating own portions sizes in relation to general health recommendations.

Propose-moi un plan pour la première partie "État des lieux" du plan stratégique de l’arbre en Bretagne. Celui-ci a pour vocation d’embrasser la thématique de l’arbre dans toutes ses manifestations sur le territoire breton (forêt, bocage, vergers, arbre en ville), et ce, dans une vision fédératrice et transversale. Il répond à trois objectifs principaux :
•	Développer la présence de l’arbre, tant en milieu urbain que dans l’espace rural 
•	Promouvoir une gestion durable de l’arbre, du bocage et de la forêt, permettant de préserver leurs fonctionnalités écologiques.
•	Renforcer les usages et produits issus de l’arbre
En somme, ce plan visera à développer une meilleure synergie entre les politiques publiques régionales, entre les acteurs et entre les politiques publiques. 请翻译下列文章Discussion
To our knowledge, this is the first study to compare individual estimates of amounts of served food with the actual weight of the food served in a laboratory setting, where less disruptive data collection techniques are applied. Other studies assessing the accuracy of estimated portion sizes have used photographs as the reference for the assessment (Huybregts et al, 2007, Turconi et al, 2005), fake food items (Bucher et al, 2011, Bucher et al, 2012, Bucher et al, 2013) or average portion size weights based on repeated measures (Ngigi, Verbeke, & Pérez-Cueto, 2011). In contrast, the present study was performed using actual food items. In addition, the use of the Intelligent Buffet allowed the exact weight of food served by each participant to be recorded in a relatively undisturbed manner.

There are a few potential sources of bias in this study, one being measurement bias. An attempt was made to limit this by calibrating the equipment used for data collection before use and by following standard laboratory procedures. Therefore, if any measurement bias were to occur, it would be systematic throughout all observations. Secondly, the sample size may have been insufficient. However, the calculated power of 0.99 for the observed mean differences of both vegetables and whole grains suggests that the sample was enough to support the rejection of the null hypothesis. Previous studies have used a similar sample size with sufficient power (Mekhmoukh, Chapelot, & Bellisle, 2012). Thus, we assume that the result of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was accurate (absence of type II error), and that it was correct to reject the null hypothesis since there was a significant difference between the two variables – the estimated and actual amount of food served.

Our findings are in agreement with similar studies conducted in a number of different countries and settings, including Norway (Uglem et al., 2008), the Netherlands (Lechner et al., 1997), Australia (Pollard et al., 2008) and Denmark (Sørensen et al., 2013), suggesting that individuals commonly have difficulties estimating food portion sizes with accuracy. The findings of a statistically significant difference between participants’ self-estimation and the actual weight of the vegetables served led to the rejection of the null hypothesis (Table 1). The participants in this study were also asked to estimate the weight of a whole grain serving in a relatively complex meal. It would be of interest to determine whether the results would have been more accurate if a simpler meal had been served (e.g. a bowl of cereal). However, the everyday diet commonly consists of prepared meals or ready-to-eat foods and individuals are often not aware of the actual composition of the foods they consume. Therefore, serving a “complex meal” is comparable with a real life situation, where participants are expected to estimate the amount of food served (Combet et al, 2013, Loh et al, 2013).

This study presents the question of whether food intake estimations that are independent of actual weighing are valid, particularly in the evaluation of adherence to healthy eating recommendations (Pérez-Cueto et al., 2012). This also underscores the importance of using alternative equipment and techniques, such as an Intelligent Buffet, in order to obtain actual data in studies measuring factors such as food intake (Bucher et al., 2012). The Intelligent Buffet presents many opportunities to conduct other studies or further research on this particular topic. In combination with video cameras, this equipment could be used for choice architectural experiments researching behaviour related to a buffet setting. For example, it could be used to investigate whether individual consumption differs in relation to the order of food items or the size of serving trays.

As seen in Table 1, there is no statistical correlation between measured and estimated values; they are independent variables meaning that there is no predictive relationship between the two measurements.

Consequently, if authors were to compare the difference between means they would probably find that the estimations are so different from the actual intake that they are neither reliable nor valid, thus supporting the use of alternative techniques such as the Intelligent Buffet when accuracy is a requirement of the research.

Generalizability of the findings is limited due to the study design and sample size. The use of a convenience sample from a university setting introduced a sample mainly consisting of higher educated participants aged between 20 and 29 years. Consequently, the results measure perception of serving size against the weight of the food served for this survey sample. A larger sample size and a different study design would need to be undertaken to explore if these findings extrapolate to the general University student community or to specific socio-economic groups within that community. The literature and the current study findings suggest the likelihood of an overestimation of portion sizes. However, further studies should be carried out before making conclusions about whether the general population is capable of accurately estimating food portion sizes and about the effects this could have on the degree of validity in studies involving self-estimation as a data collection method.

Considering that the majority of participants were highly educated people and nevertheless unable to correctly estimate the amounts of vegetables and whole grain served, and previous research highlighting that lower socioeconomic groups may find it difficult to interpret serving size recommendations, these findings may be of concern for nutrition educators (Drewnowski, Specter, 2004, Kamp et al, 2010, Robinson, 2008, Sinclair et al, 2013). Studies show that individuals from higher socio-demographic groups have a greater knowledge and comprehension of nutrition than individuals from low socio-demographic groups (Drewnowski, Specter, 2004, Pollard et al, 2008, Sinclair et al, 2013).

Furthermore, this study raises the question about whether self-estimation of portion sizes would be an appropriate way to evaluate intake of vegetables and whole grain cereals, particularly in self-serving settings, such as University Canteens, since it appears that the participants had very little ability to estimate their own intake (estimated serving vs actual serving were independent measures). Probably, this will be applicable to most other food groups, and thus this study challenges the way for instance communication towards healthy eating is delivered. It also calls for innovative ways to make the population aware of what portions are if the intention is to rely on the general ability to estimate quantities of food served or eaten.

Conclusion
The present study was the first to assess the accuracy of self-estimates of vegetables and whole grain portion sizes in a self-served meal conducted in a laboratory setting using an Intelligent Buffet combined with a quantitative questionnaire. When comparing the self-estimated amount of vegetables and whole grains with the actual amount, the analysis revealed a significant difference between the means (P < 0.001) where students’ self-reported portions were about three times bigger than the actual servings.

The study supports the use of innovative techniques such as the Intelligent Buffet. Further it supports the use of triangulation in order to obtain more precise estimations on intake and to better evaluate the real adherence to nutritional recommendations.

The questionnaires provided information on the profile of the participants and it appeared that there was little variety within the sample. Further limitations could be linked to the sample size and the methodological approach, particularly the equipment used for the data collection and data management, which had never been utilised prior to the study.

This study suggests that at least for this survey sample individuals do not provide accurate estimates of the amount of vegetables and whole grains they serve themselves on a plate. Our study findings lead us to question individuals’ ability to assess the amounts of vegetables and whole grain they serve themselves from a buffet. The degree of underestimation of servings within this small experimental group is high. On average participants assessed that they served themselves about three times what they actually did. Although there was a high awareness of the Danish 6 A Day recommendation among study participants, their ability to accurately estimate their serving size appeared to be a limited. These findings highlight the need for further research into the accuracy of self-estimated intake across the population and the implications of the overestimation of current consumption for nutrition promotion interventions.

Based on the findings of this study it is recommended that policy makers and social marketing campaign creators consider the development of more specific serving size measurements or that explicit communications e.g. regarding serves of plant foods used in nutrition education are needed to assist consumers in estimating own portions sizes in relation to general health recommendations.

def fetch_instagram_data():
    url = INSTAGRAM_GRAPH_API + "me/media?fields=id,caption,media_type,media_url,permalink,thumbnail_url,timestamp,username,like_count,impressions,comments_count&access_token=" + ACCESS_TOKEN
    response = requests.get(url)
    data = json.loads(response.text)
    return data["data"]

def process_caption(caption_text):
    desc_start_idx = caption_text.index("[Description]")
    desc_end_idx = caption_text.index("[Tags]", desc_start_idx)
    return caption_text[desc_start_idx + 12:desc_end_idx].strip()

def get_photo_id_based_on_timestamp(timestamp, photo_ids):
    date_str = datetime.strptime(timestamp, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z").strftime('%Y%m%d')
    count = photo_ids.get(date_str, 0) + 1
    photo_ids[date_str] = count
    return f"{date_str}{count}"

def get_image_overlay(media_id):
    media_url = INSTAGRAM_GRAPH_API + f"/{media_id}/children/?fields=id,media_type,media_url&access_token=" + ACCESS_TOKEN
    response = requests.get(media_url)
    if response.status_code == 200:
        data = json.loads(response.text)
        images = [child["media_url"] for child in data["data"] if child["media_type"] == "IMAGE"]
        return images
    return []

def fetch_comments(media_id):
    url = INSTAGRAM_GRAPH_API + f"/{media_id}/comments?fields=id,text,username,timestamp&access_token=" + ACCESS_TOKEN
    response = requests.get(url)
    data = json.loads(response.text)['data']
    return data

def fetch_additional_insta_data(username):
    L = instaloader.Instaloader()
    L.download_stories(userids=[username], fast_update=True, to_storyitem=None, to_receiver=None)

def create_post_widget(post_data):
    row_count = 0
    col1, col2, col3 = st.beta_columns(3)
    photo_ids = {}
    for post in post_data:
        if post["media_type"] != "IMAGE":
            continue
        media_id = get_photo_id_based_on_timestamp(post["timestamp"], photo_ids)
        st.write(f"ID: {media_id}")
        with st.beta_expander("Show Image"):

            if "children" in post:

        st.write(f"Caption: {process_caption(post['caption'])}")

        if row_count % 3 == 0:

        if row_count % 3 == 1:
            col2 = col2.container()
        if row_count % 3 == 2:
            col3 = col3.container()
        row_count += 1

The presence of missing values in the data objects is ubiquitous in practice. Missing entries could be due to various types of faults during data collection, data transfer, or data cleaning phase and may occur arbitrarily. Dealing with a data set with missing values is one of the infamous challenges in data science. The problems of filling up missing entries are often cast as optimization tasks. One such problem is the following:

You are given an m×n matrix M with each entry set to either 0 or 1 or a wildcard ∗. Furthermore, all the entries of the last (i.e., mth) row of M are set to wildcards (i.e., ∗). You are also given a non-negative integer r. The problem is to decide whether there exists an m × n matrix M¯ ∈ {0, 1} m×n (i.e., with no ∗-entry) such that

For all (i, j) ∈ {1, 2, · · · , m} × {1, 2, · · · , n} with M[i][j] ̸= ∗, M¯ [i][j] = M[i][j], and

The number of entries that are different between the last row and any other row in M¯ is at most r. More formally, for every i ∈ {1, 2, · · · , m − 1},
{j ∈ {1, 2, · · · , n} | M¯ [i][j] ̸= M¯ [m][j]} ≤ r

Nature, weather and conditions on the planet are similar to those on Earth (so far, I think so)

Way 2: Engineers' Devices. Engineers are another social class of The Children of God, capable of producing special electronic devices that allow simulating the external senses of representatives of different dimensions, so that the connection between them, even at a distance in time and space, is fast and complete in terms of the coincidence of the organs of perception of all participants in the act of communication.

One of the Carriers was the eagle Altair: a storyteller whose voice and stories fascinated. He had a special instrument, let's temporarily call it the Altair Lyre, a six-stringed elegant lyre with a body resembling a swirling sea wave. At night, retreating into the rocks, Altair took on a form that allowed him to play an instrument. During the day, being a Carrier, Altair did not accompany his voice in any way, and his sweet speech was everything that should have delighted enthusiastic passengers.

One day, a young Daughter of God Vega came to the Carrier and asked to take her several dimensions ahead. She had never felt those places before, and she wanted to find out how it was possible to learn with the help of a completely different understanding of the world, as she thought, more complete and unusual.

Vega and Altair started talking. They were concerned that since the time when their world was created (the faith of The Children of God in The Supreme-God-Demiurge was unshakable and there were several artifacts confirming its existence), no one talks about whether other worlds similar to theirs were created. And is it possible for simple Child of God to become like The Supreme-God-Demiurge? Can Vega or Altair achieve such perfection in their art that they can create worlds themselves? Once Altair heard from one of the passengers that it was possible to combine the attributes of several social classes so that the result would be “something inexpressible". For example, an element for a combination could be Altair's Lyre or his fairy tales. And Vega's…

Vega continued the craft of the Weavers' class: The Weavers planned the trajectories of the Carriers. One of her tools were Needles — they marked points in the multidimensional space of their world that Carriers had to pass through to activate their abilities and reach the right tools. Accordingly, the attributes of Vega for the necessary combination that could lead to the creation of a new world could be Needles.

Altair and Vega spent a lot of time together: Vega often traveled, and Altair seemed to inevitably, by fate itself, find himself on her way. Vega listened attentively to all his fairy tales and once admitted that she would like to hear them at night: at a time when Altair was changing his external form and playing the Lyre. Altair agreed, and from then on, once every few weeks or months, they spent a Night of Songs together. Vega brought Needles to these meetings and, instead of plotting the trajectories of future interdimensional movements with them, she clung to Altair's words, the overtones of his voice, and connected them to the place where they were. Now, with the help of Needles, pebbles, leaves of rare shrubs, sand and even fog seemed to enter into a dialogue with Altair. Vega felt almost like an Engineer: what if she and Altair could create a new world? It seems that they already have almost everything for this…

One day Altair received a special task and realized that he had to leave the dimension where Vega lived for a long time. They met again at the moment when Vega decided to go on one of her interdimensional journeys, and Altair told her the sad news: “Perhaps we will never feel each other with you again, only if the Engineers don't come to the rescue ... but now I can't tell you where to look for me, and how to contact me.” Vega was stunned, but tried to restrain herself. At parting, Altair presented her with a great gift: “without you, I don't see the point of singing. Take this Lyre and, if destined, create a new world alone.”

Vega accepted Altair's Lyre as a gift. She saw Altair off and returned home, looking at the Needles with hatred: “Am I really going to be forced to help lay routes for the rest of my days, on which we will never cross again?”

Vega plunged into the study of the art of pairing attributes — alchemy. In the end, she succeeded: by putting together the music of Altair's Lyre, Altair's songs, which Vega performed herself from now on, and what she turned into Needles, turning to Engineers for help — a toy car for transporting passengers moving along the rails (The Train) — Vega got a completely new living space. The movement of the Train for transportation, which Vega named after her attributes — the Needle, under her songs, created a special field around itself, which turned into the atmosphere of a new small planet — MHIWYA (it was in honor of her that I gave the name to the whole legend). on this planet, as Vega learns later, the seed of future life was also born.

The first people who appeared on MHIWYA were called Nomads or Voices, which is a more general term. Each of Nomads had a voice of fabulous beauty and depth, the ranges of which coincided with the ranges of the six strings of the Altair Lyre. From now on, the tales and songs of the Nomads will maintain the state of MHIWYA from the inside, while Vega continues her Eternal Divine Song of abandonment and loneliness from the outside. The nomads founded the City, and everyone they spawned became Citizens. Also, every Citizen was a Voice along the branch of the Nomad he was born with.

MHIWYA, as well as the World-of-the-Children-of-God, turned out to be multidimensional, but now communication between residents of different dimensions was carried out with the help of an Needle Train, transporting people to each other along looped rails that permeate the entire new planet. Tiny villages formed around the rails at special points where the Train moved from one dimension to another. The villages were inhabited by Fishermen — those who, at the right moment, turned the arrows on the rails and ensured the correct transition of the Train from dimension to dimension.

The Needle rails were unstable: since the Train moves forever, the rails are constantly being rebuilt, but the path along them remains looped. Necessarily on its way, the Needle falls into many Points where space allows you to move from one dimension to another.

Here are the docs for the pain 008.001.02 format, write me a conversion library for js that can take an csv as input and send back an xml with the correct iso 20022 format

---

Input XML File for PAIN.008.001.02
This page contains a description of the input XML file for the PAIN.008.001.02 specification, which is used for ACH Direct Debit (ACH Pull) CCD and PPD payments.

    The following is a high-level example of a PAIN.008.001.02 input XML file:

    XML

    <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" ?>
<Document xmlns="urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:pain.008.001.02">
    <CstmrDrctDbtInitn>
    <GrpHdr>
...
</GrpHdr>
<PmtInf>
    ...
</PmtInf>
</CstmrDrctDbtInitn>
</Document>
The root document tag for the input file is CstmrDrctDbtInitn. It contains a Group Header and at least one Payment Information building block (corresponding to a batch). The Group Header contains metadata that relates to all the batches in the file. Each batch contains meta data for all the transactions within.

    Group Header (GrpHdr)
Your XML Input file must include a group header using the GrpHdr building block. This building block is only present once in a file and contains a set of characteristics shared by all the individual instructions included in the message.

    XML

<GrpHdr>
<MsgId>ABCDEFG090301</MsgId>
<CreDtTm>2013-08-28T17:12:44</CreDtTm>
<NbOfTxs>5</NbOfTxs>
<CtrlSum>43236.93</CtrlSum>
<InitgPty>
    ...
</InitgPty>
</GrpHdr>
Here's an explanation of the different tags in the GrpHdr block as shown above:

MsgId: An ID number for the message, which you assign before sending the file to CRB. Best practice: Use a new for each file.**
CreDtTm: The date and time the payment instruction was created.
    NbOfTxs: The total number of transaction instruction blocks in the message. Each instruction corresponds to one transaction, and will form a separate instruction block. For more information on the transaction instruction blocks, see the Direct Debit Transaction Information section below.
    CtrlSum: The total amount (as a number) of all the instructions included in the file, irrespective of currencies, used as a control sum. Note: Unicorn currently supports USD only.
    InitgPty: Indicates the party initiating the transfer. This is the party initiating the credit transfer on behalf of the debtor. See the Initiating Party section that follows for more details on the tags inside the InitgPty block.
    Note: All the above elements in the GrpHdr block are required.

    Initiating Party (InitgPty)
The Initiating Party is the party initiating the payment. This is the party that initiates the credit transfer on behalf of the debtor.

    XML

<InitgPty>
<Nm>John Doe Corporation</Nm>
<Id>
    <OrgId>
        <Othr>
            <Id>0123456789</Id>
        </Othr>
    </OrgId>
</Id>
</InitgPty>
Here's an explanation of the different tags in the InitgPty block as shown above:

Nm: Name by which the originating party is known and which is usually used to identify that party.
    Id: Identifier. The parent element of the OrgId element containing the identifying information about the initiating party.
    OrgId: Organization Identification block containing the initiating party's identification in its child elements.
Othr: A block containing the initiating party's identification in a child element.
Id: The unique and unambiguous identifier the initiating party, which can be an organization or an individual person.
    Note: All the above elements in the InitgPty block are required.

    Payment Information (PmtInf)
The PmtInf block contains payment information per batch in your file. You must include at least one PmtInf block in your file. In most cases the input file contains only one PmtInf block, with one set of payment instructions. This enables you to indicate general properties (such as execution date, creditor information, and credited account) once at the level of the PmtInf block.

    You might want to use multiple PmtInf blocks if the file includes instructions to credit more than one account. In that case, you need a PmtInf block for each account that is going to be credited.

    XML

<PmtInf>
<PmtInfId>DOMC10000025</PmtInfId>
<PmtMtd>DD</PmtMtd>
<BtchBookg>false</BtchBookg>
<NbOfTxs>5</NbOfTxs>
<CtrlSum>12.01</CtrlSum>
<PmtTpInf>
    ...
</PmtTpInf>
<ReqdColltnDt>2020-08-21</ReqdColltnDt>
<Cdtr>
    ...
</Cdtr>
<CdtrAcct>
    ...
</CdtrAcct>
<CdtrAgt>
    ...
</CdtrAgt>
<DrctDbtTxInf>
    ...
</DrctDbtTxInf>
</PmtInf>
Below is an explanation of the different top-level tags and blocks found in the PmtInf block as shown above. These tags and blocks appear once for each PmtInf block, except for the DrctDbtTxInf block, which can appear multiple times, representing multiple transactions. Each of the other tags and blocks applies to all DrctDbtTxInf blocks that appear in the PmtInf block:

    PmtInf: This block contains payment information, such as creditor and payment type information. You can use this block repeatedly within the same input file. Note: One or more instances of the PmtInf element is required.
    PmtInfId: The unique ID number for this batch, which is assigned by the originating party. Note: This element is required.
    PmtMtd: Payment Method. For direct debit transactions you should define it as "DD". Note: This element is required.
    BtchBookg: Defines how CRB should handle the debit. If the tag is set to "TRUE", then all debit instructions will be handled as one consolidated debit. If the tag is set to "FALSE", it means that you want each debit to be handled separately. Note: Currently the system will always behave as if the value is "FALSE".
    NbOfTxs: The number of transactions within this batch. Note: This element is required.
    CtrlSum: The sum total of all instructions within this batch, irrespective of currencies, used as a control sum. Note: Unicorn currently supports "USD" only. Note: This element is required.
    PmtTpInf: The Payment Type Information block, including a priority level. See the Payment Type Information section below for more details on the PmtTpInf block. Note: This element is required.
    ReqdColltnDt: Requested Collection Date. The date on which the originator's account is to be debited. This tag currently supports current dates. Support for future dates will come in a future release. Note: This element is required.

1. Both are finite: Time and life are limited resources. We cannot extend the time we have, nor can we extend our lives indefinitely. We must make choices about how to spend our time and live our lives within these constraints.

2. Continuous and irreversible: Both time and life move forward in a continuous manner, and we cannot go back in time or reverse the aging process. We must learn from our past experiences and take that knowledge into the future as we move through life and time.

3. Change and growth: Time and life are characterized by change, growth, and development. As time passes, we grow older, and our life experiences change us. We develop new skills, learn new things, and go through different stages of life.

4. Impact on experiences and memories: Our perception of time influences our experiences and memories throughout life. Our memories are organized in terms of time, and as time passes, our perspectives on past events may change.

5. Both are valuable: Time and life are both precious commodities that people often take for granted until they become scarce. We should aim to use our time wisely and make the most of the life we are given.

6. Unpredictability: Neither time nor life can be predicted with certainty. While we can plan for the future and set goals, unexpected events may disrupt our plans or alter the course of our lives.

7. Shared experience: Time and life are universal experiences that every human being shares. Regardless of our background, culture, or location, we all live our lives within the confines of time, and we all experience the various stages of life.

8. Subjective perception: Our perception of time and life can differ greatly depending on our individual experiences, beliefs, and values. What may seem like a long time to one person may feel like a short time to another, and the value placed on one’s life can vary widely across different cultures and individuals.

Input XML File for PAIN.008.001.02
This page contains a description of the input XML file for the PAIN.008.001.02 specification, which is used for ACH Direct Debit (ACH Pull) CCD and PPD payments.

The following is a high-level example of a PAIN.008.001.02 input XML file:

XML

<?xml version=“1.0” encoding=“UTF-8” ?>
<Document xmlns=“urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:pain.008.001.02”>
<CstmrDrctDbtInitn>
<GrpHdr>
…
</GrpHdr>
<PmtInf>
…
</PmtInf>
</CstmrDrctDbtInitn>
</Document>
The root document tag for the input file is CstmrDrctDbtInitn. It contains a Group Header and at least one Payment Information building block (corresponding to a batch). The Group Header contains metadata that relates to all the batches in the file. Each batch contains meta data for all the transactions within.

Group Header (GrpHdr)
Your XML Input file must include a group header using the GrpHdr building block. This building block is only present once in a file and contains a set of characteristics shared by all the individual instructions included in the message.

XML

<GrpHdr>
<MsgId>ABCDEFG090301</MsgId>
<CreDtTm>2013-08-28T17:12:44</CreDtTm>
<NbOfTxs>5</NbOfTxs>
<CtrlSum>43236.93</CtrlSum>
<InitgPty>
…
</InitgPty>
</GrpHdr>
Here’s an explanation of the different tags in the GrpHdr block as shown above:

MsgId: An ID number for the message, which you assign before sending the file to CRB. Best practice: Use a new for each file.**
CreDtTm: The date and time the payment instruction was created.
NbOfTxs: The total number of transaction instruction blocks in the message. Each instruction corresponds to one transaction, and will form a separate instruction block. For more information on the transaction instruction blocks, see the Direct Debit Transaction Information section below.
CtrlSum: The total amount (as a number) of all the instructions included in the file, irrespective of currencies, used as a control sum. Note: Unicorn currently supports USD only.
InitgPty: Indicates the party initiating the transfer. This is the party initiating the credit transfer on behalf of the debtor. See the Initiating Party section that follows for more details on the tags inside the InitgPty block.
Note: All the above elements in the GrpHdr block are required.

Initiating Party (InitgPty)
The Initiating Party is the party initiating the payment. This is the party that initiates the credit transfer on behalf of the debtor.

XML

<InitgPty>
<Nm>John Doe Corporation</Nm>
<Id>
<OrgId>
<Othr>
<Id>0123456789</Id>
</Othr>
</OrgId>
</Id>
</InitgPty>
Here’s an explanation of the different tags in the InitgPty block as shown above:

Nm: Name by which the originating party is known and which is usually used to identify that party.
Id: Identifier. The parent element of the OrgId element containing the identifying information about the initiating party.
OrgId: Organization Identification block containing the initiating party’s identification in its child elements.
Othr: A block containing the initiating party’s identification in a child element.
Id: The unique and unambiguous identifier the initiating party, which can be an organization or an individual person.
Note: All the above elements in the InitgPty block are required.

Payment Information (PmtInf)
The PmtInf block contains payment information per batch in your file. You must include at least one PmtInf block in your file. In most cases the input file contains only one PmtInf block, with one set of payment instructions. This enables you to indicate general properties (such as execution date, creditor information, and credited account) once at the level of the PmtInf block.

You might want to use multiple PmtInf blocks if the file includes instructions to credit more than one account. In that case, you need a PmtInf block for each account that is going to be credited.

XML

<PmtInf>
<PmtInfId>DOMC10000025</PmtInfId>
<PmtMtd>DD</PmtMtd>
<BtchBookg>false</BtchBookg>
<NbOfTxs>5</NbOfTxs>
<CtrlSum>12.01</CtrlSum>
<PmtTpInf>
…
</PmtTpInf>
<ReqdColltnDt>2020-08-21</ReqdColltnDt>
<Cdtr>
…
</Cdtr>
<CdtrAcct>
…
</CdtrAcct>
<CdtrAgt>
…
</CdtrAgt>
<DrctDbtTxInf>
…
</DrctDbtTxInf>
</PmtInf>
Below is an explanation of the different top-level tags and blocks found in the PmtInf block as shown above. These tags and blocks appear once for each PmtInf block, except for the DrctDbtTxInf block, which can appear multiple times, representing multiple transactions. Each of the other tags and blocks applies to all DrctDbtTxInf blocks that appear in the PmtInf block:

PmtInf: This block contains payment information, such as creditor and payment type information. You can use this block repeatedly within the same input file. Note: One or more instances of the PmtInf element is required.
PmtInfId: The unique ID number for this batch, which is assigned by the originating party. Note: This element is required.
PmtMtd: Payment Method. For direct debit transactions you should define it as “DD”. Note: This element is required.
BtchBookg: Defines how CRB should handle the debit. If the tag is set to “TRUE”, then all debit instructions will be handled as one consolidated debit. If the tag is set to “FALSE”, it means that you want each debit to be handled separately. Note: Currently the system will always behave as if the value is “FALSE”.
NbOfTxs: The number of transactions within this batch. Note: This element is required.
CtrlSum: The sum total of all instructions within this batch, irrespective of currencies, used as a control sum. Note: Unicorn currently supports “USD” only. Note: This element is required.
PmtTpInf: The Payment Type Information block, including a priority level. See the Payment Type Information section below for more details on the PmtTpInf block. Note: This element is required.
ReqdColltnDt: Requested Collection Date. The date on which the originator’s account is to be debited. This tag currently supports current dates. Support for future dates will come in a future release. Note: This element is required.
Cdtr: Creditor block. Contains the name and postal address of the originator. See the Creditor section below for an example of the Cdtr block. Note: This element is required.
CdtrAcct: Creditor Account. The account of the originator that will be credited. See the Creditor Account section below for more details on the CdtrAcct block. Note: This element is required.
CdtrAgt: Creditor Agent block. Details on the creditor’s financial institution. See the Creditor Agent section below for more details on the CdtrAgt block. Note: This element is required.
DrctDbtTxInf: Direct Debit Transaction Information. Includes elements related to the debit side of the transaction, such as debtor and remittance information. This block can appear multiple times within the same PmtInf block. See the Direct Debit Transaction Information section below for more details on the DrctDbtTxInf block. Note: One or more of the CdtTrfTxInf element is required.
Payment Type Information (PmtTpInf)
The PmtTpInf block contains information on the payment type.

XML

<PmtTpInf>
<SvcLvl>
<Cd>NURG</Cd>
</SvcLvl>
<LclInstrm>
<Prtry>CCD</Prtry>
</LclInstrm>
</PmtTpInf>
Here’s an explanation of the different tags in the PmtTpInf block as shown in the examples above:

SvcLvl: Service Level. Contains the payment urgency level (Cd) in a child element.
Cd: Code: Payment urgency level. Note: This element is required. For direct debit transactions this has a fixed value of “NURG”.
LclInstrm: Local Instrument. Used to specify a local instrument, local clearing option and/or to further qualify the service or service level. Note: This element is required.
Prtry: Proprietary. Note: This element is required. The value must be the ACH Pull type (“CCD” or “PPD”).
Creditor (Cdtr)
The Cdtr block contains information on the name, postal address and ID of the originator (creditor).

XML

<Cdtr>
<Nm>John Doe Corporation</Nm>
<PstlAdr>
<Ctry>US</Ctry>
<AdrLine>999 Any Street, 13th Floor</AdrLine>
<AdrLine>99999 Anytown</AdrLine>
</PstlAdr>
<Id>
<OrgId>
<Othr>
<Id>0123456789</Id>
</Othr>
</OrgId>
</Id>
</Cdtr>
Nm: Creditor name.
PstlAdr: A block containing the postal address of the creditor, including country and address lines.
Id: Identification block, containing information used to identify the creditor in child elements.
OrgId: Organization Identification block containing the creditor identification in its child elements.
Othr: A block containing the creditor identification in a child element.
Id: A unique and unambiguous identifier of the creditor. This ID is identical to the Id field in the InitgPty block described above.
Creditor Account (CdtrAcct)
The CdtrAccount block contains information on the account of the originator that will be credited.

XML

<CdtrAcct>
<Id>
<Othr>
<Id>0123456789</Id>
</Othr>
</Id>
<Ccy>USD</Ccy>
</CdtrAcct>
Here’s an explanation of the different tags in the CdtrAccount block as shown above:

Id: The sub-block containing the creditor’s account identification information.
Othr: The sub-block containing the creditor’s Id tag.
Id: The unique identifier of the creditor’s account.
Ccy: Currency. The ISO currency code of the debtor’s account.
Note: All the above elements in the CdtrAcct block are required.

Creditor Agent (CdtrAgt)
The CdtrAgt block contains information on the originator’s financial institution.

XML

<CdtrAgt>
<FinInstnId>
<ClrSysMmbId>
<MmbId>123456789</MmbId>
</ClrSysMmbId>
<PstlAdr>
<Ctry>US</Ctry>
</PstlAdr>
</FinInstnId>
</CdtrAgt>
Here’s an explanation of the different tags in the CdtrAgt block as shown above:

FinInstnId: Financial Institution Identification sub-block.
ClrSysMmbId: Clearing System Member Identification sub-block. Contains Information used to identify a member within a clearing system.
MmbId: Member Identification: Identifier (routing number) of the creditor’s financial institution in the creditor’s clearing system. For Direct Debit, this value must always be CRB’s routing number (021214891).
PstlAdr: Postal Address sub-block.
Ctry: Country code. The country code for the debtor’s financial institution.
Note: All the above elements in the CdtrAgt block are required.

Direct Debit Transaction Information (DrctDbtTxInf)
The DrctDbtTxInf block includes elements related to the debit side of the transaction, such as debitor and remittance information for the transaction. You can use this block repeatedly within the same PmtInf block. The number of occurrences of the DrctDbtTxInf block within a file is indicated by the NbOfTxs field in the Group Header (GrpHdr).

XML

<DrctDbtTxInf>
<PmtId>
<EndToEndId>100DDEB000000</EndToEndId>
</PmtId>
<InstdAmt Ccy=“USD”>0.01</InstdAmt>
<DbtrAgt>
<FinInstnId>
<ClrSysMmbId>
<MmbId>123456789</MmbId>
</ClrSysMmbId>
<Nm>DUMMY</Nm>
<PstlAdr>
<Ctry>US</Ctry>
</PstlAdr>
</FinInstnId>
</DbtrAgt>
<Dbtr>
<Nm>John Doe</Nm>
<PstlAdr>
<Ctry>US</Ctry>
</PstlAdr>
</Dbtr>
<DbtrAcct>
<Id>
<Othr>
<Id>01234567890</Id>
</Othr>
</Id>
</DbtrAcct>
<RmtInf>
<Ustrd>Testing</Ustrd>
</RmtInf>
</DrctDbtTxInf>
Here’s an explanation of the different tags in the DrctDbtTxInf block as shown above:

PmtId: Payment Identification sub-block. Provides identifying information regarding the transaction in child elements. Note: This element is required.
EndToEndId: End to End Identification: End-to-end reference number of the credit transfer. This information is sent to the beneficiary. Note: This element is required.
InstdAmt: Instructed Amount. The amount of the credit transfer in the indicated currency. Note: This element is required.
DbtrAgt: Debtor Agent block. Details on the debtor’s financial institution for the transaction. See the Debtor Agent section below for more details on the DbtrAgt block. Note: This element is required.
Dbtr: The debtor sub-block. Contains details on the debtor for the transaction, including Nm (name) and PstlAdr (postal address) elements. Note: The Dbtr block and its Nm element are required. The PstlAdr element is not required.
DbtrAcct: Debtor account sub-block for the transaction, containing the debtor account number in its child elements. Note: This element is required.
Id: Identification sub-block. Contains an identification of the debtor account in child elements. Note: This element is required.
Othr: Sub-block containing the debtor’s Id tag. Note: This element is required.
Id: The unique identifier of the debtor’s account. Note: This element is required.
RmtInf: The remittance information to send along with the transaction. Note: This element is required for ACH Direct Debit.
Ustrd: Unstructured description of the transaction. Note: This element is required.
Debtor Agent (DbtrAgt)
The DbtrAgt block contains information on the debtor’s financial institution.

XML

<DbtrAgt>
<FinInstnId>
<ClrSysMmbId>
<MmbId>123456789</MmbId>
</ClrSysMmbId>
<Nm>John Doe Bank</Nm>
<PstlAdr>
<Ctry>US</Ctry>
</PstlAdr>
</FinInstnId>
</DbtrAgt>
Here’s an explanation of the different tags in the DbtrAgt block as shown above:

FinInstnId: Financial Institution Identification sub-block.
ClrSysMmbId: Clearing System Member Identification sub-block. Contains Information used to identify a member within a clearing system.
MmbId: Member Identification: Identification (routing number) of the debtor’s financial institution in the debtor’s clearing system.
Nm: Name of the debtor’s financial institution.
PstlAdr: Postal Address sub-block.
Ctry: Country code. The ISO country code for the creditor’s financial institution.
Note: All the above elements in the DbtrAgt block are required.
